sentence: In modern molecular biology and genetics, the genome is the genetic material of an organism.

sentence: Symbiosis (from Greek σύν "together" and βίωσις "living") is close and often long-term interaction between two different biological species.

sentence: In 1879, the German mycologist Heinrich Anton de Bary defined it as "the living together of unlike organisms."

sentence: The definition of symbiosis has varied among scientists.

sentence: Some believe symbiosis should only refer to persistent mutualisms, while others believe it should apply to any type of persistent biological interaction (in other words mutualistic, commensalistic, or parasitic).

sentence: After 130 years of debate, current biology and ecology textbooks now use the latter "de Bary" definition or an even broader definition (where symbiosis means all species interactions), with the restrictive definition no longer used (in other words, symbiosis means mutualism).

sentence: Some symbiotic relationships are obligate, meaning that both symbionts entirely depend on each other for survival.

sentence: For example, many lichens consist of fungal and photosynthetic symbionts that cannot live on their own.

sentence: Others are facultative (optional): they can, but do not have to live with the other organism.

sentence: Symbiotic relationships include those associations in which one organism lives on another (ectosymbiosis, such as mistletoe), or where one partner lives inside the other (endosymbiosis, such as lactobacilli and other bacteria in humans or Symbiodinium in corals).

sentence: Symbiosis is also classified by physical attachment of the organisms; symbiosis in which the organisms have bodily union is called conjunctive symbiosis, and symbiosis in which they are not in union is called disjunctive symbiosis.

sentence: Commensalism describes a relationship between two living organisms where one benefits and the other is not significantly harmed or helped.

sentence: Amensalism is the type of relationship that exists where one species is inhibited or completely obliterated and one is unaffected.

sentence: [citation needed] There are two types of amensalism, competition and antibiosis.

sentence: A web browser (commonly referred to as a browser) is a software application for retrieving, presenting, and traversing information resources on the World Wide Web.

sentence: The primary purpose of a web browser is to bring information resources to the user ("retrieval" or "fetching"), allowing them to view the information ("display", "rendering"), and then access other information ("navigation", "following links").

sentence: Catalan (/ˈkætəlæn/; autonym: català [kətəˈla] or [kataˈla]) is a Romance language named for its origins in Catalonia, in what is northeastern Spain and adjoining parts of France.

sentence: Daylight saving time (DST) or summer time is the practice of advancing clocks during summer months by one hour so that in the evening daylight is experienced an hour longer, while sacrificing normal sunrise times.

sentence: Germany and Austria-Hungary organized the first nationwide implementation, starting on 30 April 1916.

sentence: The practice has received both advocacy and criticism.

sentence: Putting clocks forward benefits retailing, sports, and other activities that exploit sunlight after working hours, but can cause problems for evening entertainment and for other activities tied to sunlight, such as farming.

sentence: Although some early proponents of DST aimed to reduce evening use of incandescent lighting, which used to be a primary use of electricity, modern heating and cooling usage patterns differ greatly and research about how DST affects energy use is limited or contradictory.

sentence: Computer software can often adjust clocks automatically, but policy changes by various jurisdictions of the dates and timings of DST may be confusing.

sentence: Industrialized societies generally follow a clock-based schedule for daily activities that do not change throughout the course of the year.
label: sentence

sentence: The time of day that individuals begin and end work or school, and the coordination of mass transit, for example, usually remain constant year-round.
label: sentence

sentence: In contrast, an agrarian society's daily routines for work and personal conduct are more likely governed by the length of daylight hours and by solar time, which change seasonally because of the Earth's axial tilt.

sentence: North and south of the tropics daylight lasts longer in summer and shorter in winter, the effect becoming greater as one moves away from the tropics.
label: sentence

sentence: By synchronously resetting all clocks in a region to one hour ahead of Standard Time (one hour "fast"), individuals who follow such a year-round schedule will wake an hour earlier than they would have otherwise; they will begin and complete daily work routines an hour earlier, and they will have available to them an extra hour of daylight after their workday activities.

sentence: However, they will have one less hour of daylight at the start of each day, making the policy less practical during winter.

sentence: While the times of sunrise and sunset change at roughly equal rates as the seasons change, proponents of Daylight Saving Time argue that most people prefer a greater increase in daylight hours after the typical "nine-to-five" workday.

sentence: Supporters have also argued that DST decreases energy consumption by reducing the need for lighting and heating, but the actual effect on overall energy use is heavily disputed.

sentence: Tristan da Cunha /ˈtrɪstən də ˈkuːnjə/, colloquially Tristan, is both a remote group of volcanic islands in the south Atlantic Ocean and the main island of that group.

sentence: Political corruption is the use of powers by government officials for illegitimate private gain.

sentence: A treaty is an agreement under international law entered into by actors in international law, namely sovereign states and international organizations.
label: sentence

sentence: A treaty may also be known as an (international) agreement, protocol, covenant, convention, pact, or exchange of letters, among other terms.
label: sentence

sentence: Regardless of terminology, all of these forms of agreements are, under international law, equally considered treaties and the rules are the same.
label: sentence

sentence: Treaties can be loosely compared to contracts: both are means of willing parties assuming obligations among themselves, and a party to either that fails to live up to their obligations can be held liable under international law.
label: sentence

sentence: A treaty is an official, express written agreement that states use to legally bind themselves.
label: sentence

sentence: A treaty is the official document which expresses that agreement in words; and it is also the objective outcome of a ceremonial occasion which acknowledges the parties and their defined relationships.
label: sentence

sentence: Since the late 19th century, most treaties have followed a fairly consistent format.
label: sentence

sentence: A treaty typically begins with a preamble describing the contracting parties and their joint objectives in executing the treaty, as well as summarizing any underlying events (such as a war).
label: sentence

sentence: Modern preambles are sometimes structured as a single very long sentence formatted into multiple paragraphs for readability, in which each of the paragraphs begins with a verb (desiring, recognizing, having, and so on).
label: sentence

sentence: The contracting parties' full names or sovereign titles are often included in the preamble, along with the full names and titles of their representatives, and a boilerplate clause about how their representatives have communicated (or exchanged) their full powers (i.e., the official documents appointing them to act on behalf of their respective states) and found them in good or proper form.
label: sentence

sentence: After the preamble comes numbered articles, which contain the substance of the parties' actual agreement.
label: sentence

sentence: Each article heading usually encompasses a paragraph.
label: sentence

sentence: A long treaty may further group articles under chapter headings.
label: sentence

sentence: Modern treaties, regardless of subject matter, usually contain articles governing where the final authentic copies of the treaty will be deposited and how any subsequent disputes as to their interpretation will be peacefully resolved.
label: sentence

sentence: The end of a treaty, the eschatocol (or closing protocol), is often signaled by a clause like "in witness whereof" or "in faith whereof," the parties have affixed their signatures, followed by the words "DONE at," then the site(s) of the treaty's execution and the date(s) of its execution.
label: sentence

sentence: The date is typically written in its most formal, longest possible form.
label: sentence

sentence: For example, the Charter of the United Nations was "DONE at the city of San Francisco the twenty-sixth day of June, one thousand nine hundred and forty-five."
label: sentence

sentence: If the treaty is executed in multiple copies in different languages, that fact is always noted, and is followed by a stipulation that the versions in different languages are equally authentic.
label: sentence

sentence: The signatures of the parties' representatives follow at the very end.
label: sentence

sentence: When the text of a treaty is later reprinted, such as in a collection of treaties currently in effect, an editor will often append the dates on which the respective parties ratified the treaty and on which it came into effect for each party.
label: sentence

sentence: Bilateral treaties are concluded between two states or entities.
label: sentence

sentence: It is possible, however, for a bilateral treaty to have more than two parties; consider for instance the bilateral treaties between Switzerland and the European Union (EU) following the Swiss rejection of the European Economic Area agreement.
label: sentence

sentence: Each of these treaties has seventeen parties.
label: sentence

sentence: These however are still bilateral, not multilateral, treaties.
label: sentence

sentence: The parties are divided into two groups, the Swiss ("on the one part") and the EU and its member states ("on the other part").
label: sentence

sentence: The treaty establishes rights and obligations between the Swiss and the EU and the member states severally—it does not establish any rights and obligations amongst the EU and its member states.
label: sentence

sentence: [citation needed]
label: sentence

sentence: A multilateral treaty is concluded among several countries.
label: sentence

sentence: The agreement establishes rights and obligations between each party and every other party.
label: sentence

sentence: Multilateral treaties are often regional.
label: sentence

sentence: [citation needed] Treaties of "mutual guarantee" are international compacts, e.g., the Treaty of Locarno which guarantees each signatory against attack from another.
label: sentence

sentence: Reservations are essentially caveats to a state's acceptance of a treaty.
label: sentence

sentence: Reservations are unilateral statements purporting to exclude or to modify the legal obligation and its effects on the reserving state.
label: sentence

sentence: These must be included at the time of signing or ratification, i.e.
label: sentence

sentence: "a party cannot add a reservation after it has already joined a treaty".
label: sentence

sentence: Originally, international law was unaccepting of treaty reservations, rejecting them unless all parties to the treaty accepted the same reservations.
label: sentence

sentence: However, in the interest of encouraging the largest number of states to join treaties, a more permissive rule regarding reservations has emerged.
label: sentence

sentence: While some treaties still expressly forbid any reservations, they are now generally permitted to the extent that they are not inconsistent with the goals and purposes of the treaty.
label: sentence

sentence: When a state limits its treaty obligations through reservations, other states party to that treaty have the option to accept those reservations, object to them, or object and oppose them.
label: sentence

sentence: If the state accepts them (or fails to act at all), both the reserving state and the accepting state are relieved of the reserved legal obligation as concerns their legal obligations to each other (accepting the reservation does not change the accepting state's legal obligations as concerns other parties to the treaty).
label: sentence

sentence: If the state opposes, the parts of the treaty affected by the reservation drop out completely and no longer create any legal obligations on the reserving and accepting state, again only as concerns each other.
label: sentence

sentence: Finally, if the state objects and opposes, there are no legal obligations under that treaty between those two state parties whatsoever.
label: sentence

sentence: The objecting and opposing state essentially refuses to acknowledge the reserving state is a party to the treaty at all.
label: sentence

sentence: There are three ways an existing treaty can be amended.
label: sentence

sentence: First, formal amendment requires State parties to the treaty to go through the ratification process all over again.
label: sentence

sentence: The re-negotiation of treaty provisions can be long and protracted, and often some parties to the original treaty will not become parties to the amended treaty.
label: sentence

sentence: When determining the legal obligations of states, one party to the original treaty and one a party to the amended treaty, the states will only be bound by the terms they both agreed upon.
label: sentence

sentence: Treaties can also be amended informally by the treaty executive council when the changes are only procedural, technical change in customary international law can also amend a treaty, where state behavior evinces a new interpretation of the legal obligations under the treaty.
label: sentence

sentence: Minor corrections to a treaty may be adopted by a procès-verbal; but a procès-verbal is generally reserved for changes to rectify obvious errors in the text adopted, i.e.
label: sentence

sentence: where the text adopted does not correctly reflect the intention of the parties adopting it.

sentence: In international law and international relations, a protocol is generally a treaty or international agreement that supplements a previous treaty or international agreement.

sentence: Treaties may be seen as 'self-executing', in that merely becoming a party puts the treaty and all of its obligations in action.
label: sentence

sentence: Other treaties may be non-self-executing and require 'implementing legislation'—a change in the domestic law of a state party that will direct or enable it to fulfill treaty obligations.

sentence: The language of treaties, like that of any law or contract, must be interpreted when the wording does not seem clear or it is not immediately apparent how it should be applied in a perhaps unforeseen circumstance.

sentence: Organisms inherit their genes from their parents.

sentence: According to Mendelian inheritance, variations in an organism's phenotype (observable physical and behavioral characteristics) are due in part to variations in its genotype (particular set of genes).

sentence: For example, if the allele specifying tall stems in pea plants is dominant over the allele specifying short stems, then pea plants that inherit one tall allele from one parent and one short allele from the other parent will also have tall stems.

sentence: Mendel's work demonstrated that alleles assort independently in the production of gametes, or germ cells, ensuring variation in the next generation.

sentence: Although Mendelian inheritance remains a good model for many traits determined by single genes (including a number of well-known genetic disorders) it does not include the physical processes of DNA replication and cell division.

sentence: The growth, development, and reproduction of organisms relies on cell division, or the process by which a single cell divides into two usually identical daughter cells.

sentence: This requires first making a duplicate copy of every gene in the genome in a process called DNA replication.

sentence: :5.2 The copies are made by specialized enzymes known as DNA polymerases, which "read" one strand of the double-helical DNA, known as the template strand, and synthesize a new complementary strand.

sentence: :18.2 In prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) this usually occurs via a relatively simple process called binary fission, in which each circular genome attaches to the cell membrane and is separated into the daughter cells as the membrane invaginates to split the cytoplasm into two membrane-bound portions.

sentence: When multiple different alleles for a gene are present in a species's population it is called polymorphic.

sentence: Genes with a most recent common ancestor, and thus a shared evolutionary ancestry, are known as homologs.

sentence: All vertebrates have a blood–brain barrier that allows metabolism inside the brain to operate differently from metabolism in other parts of the body.

sentence: The invention of electronic computers in the 1940s, along with the development of mathematical information theory, led to a realization that brains can potentially be understood as information processing systems.

sentence: This concept formed the basis of the field of cybernetics, and eventually gave rise to the field now known as computational neuroscience.

sentence: The earliest attempts at cybernetics were somewhat crude in that they treated the brain as essentially a digital computer in disguise, as for example in John von Neumann's 1958 book, The Computer and the Brain.

sentence: Over the years, though, accumulating information about the electrical responses of brain cells recorded from behaving animals has steadily moved theoretical concepts in the direction of increasing realism.

sentence: The essence of the information processing approach is to try to understand brain function in terms of information flow and implementation of algorithms.

sentence: One of the most influential early contributions was a 1959 paper titled What the frog's eye tells the frog's brain: the paper examined the visual responses of neurons in the retina and optic tectum of frogs, and came to the conclusion that some neurons in the tectum of the frog are wired to combine elementary responses in a way that makes them function as "bug perceivers".

sentence: A few years later David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel discovered cells in the primary visual cortex of monkeys that become active when sharp edges move across specific points in the field of view—a discovery for which they won a Nobel Prize.

sentence: Follow-up studies in higher-order visual areas found cells that detect binocular disparity, color, movement, and aspects of shape, with areas located at increasing distances from the primary visual cortex showing increasingly complex responses.

sentence: Other investigations of brain areas unrelated to vision have revealed cells with a wide variety of response correlates, some related to memory, some to abstract types of cognition such as space.

sentence: Furthermore, even single neurons appear to be complex and capable of performing computations.

sentence: So, brain models that don't reflect this are arguably too abstractive to be representative of brain operation; models that do try to capture this are very computationally expensive and arguably intractable with present computational resources.

sentence: One of the primary functions of a brain is to extract biologically relevant information from sensory inputs.
label: sentence

sentence: The human brain is provided with information about light, sound, the chemical composition of the atmosphere, temperature, head orientation, limb position, the chemical composition of the bloodstream, and more.
label: sentence

sentence: In other animals additional senses may be present, such as the infrared heat-sense of snakes, the magnetic field sense of some birds, or the electric field sense of some types of fish.
label: sentence

sentence: Moreover, other animals may develop existing sensory systems in new ways, such as the adaptation by bats of the auditory sense into a form of sonar.
label: sentence

sentence: One way or another, all of these sensory modalities are initially detected by specialized sensors that project signals into the brain.
label: sentence

sentence: Each sensory system begins with specialized receptor cells, such as light-receptive neurons in the retina of the eye, vibration-sensitive neurons in the cochlea of the ear, or pressure-sensitive neurons in the skin.
label: sentence

sentence: The axons of sensory receptor cells travel into the spinal cord or brain, where they transmit their signals to a first-order sensory nucleus dedicated to one specific sensory modality.
label: sentence

sentence: This primary sensory nucleus sends information to higher-order sensory areas that are dedicated to the same modality.
label: sentence

sentence: Eventually, via a way-station in the thalamus, the signals are sent to the cerebral cortex, where they are processed to extract biologically relevant features, and integrated with signals coming from other sensory systems.

sentence: Motor systems are areas of the brain that are directly or indirectly involved in producing body movements, that is, in activating muscles.
label: sentence

sentence: Except for the muscles that control the eye, which are driven by nuclei in the midbrain, all the voluntary muscles in the body are directly innervated by motor neurons in the spinal cord and hindbrain.
label: sentence

sentence: Spinal motor neurons are controlled both by neural circuits intrinsic to the spinal cord, and by inputs that descend from the brain.
label: sentence

sentence: The intrinsic spinal circuits implement many reflex responses, and contain pattern generators for rhythmic movements such as walking or swimming.
label: sentence

sentence: The descending connections from the brain allow for more sophisticated control.
label: sentence

sentence: The brain contains several motor areas that project directly to the spinal cord.
label: sentence

sentence: At the lowest level are motor areas in the medulla and pons, which control stereotyped movements such as walking, breathing, or swallowing.
label: sentence

sentence: At a higher level are areas in the midbrain, such as the red nucleus, which is responsible for coordinating movements of the arms and legs.
label: sentence

sentence: At a higher level yet is the primary motor cortex, a strip of tissue located at the posterior edge of the frontal lobe.
label: sentence

sentence: The primary motor cortex sends projections to the subcortical motor areas, but also sends a massive projection directly to the spinal cord, through the pyramidal tract.
label: sentence

sentence: This direct corticospinal projection allows for precise voluntary control of the fine details of movements.
label: sentence

sentence: Other motor-related brain areas exert secondary effects by projecting to the primary motor areas.
label: sentence

sentence: Among the most important secondary areas are the premotor cortex, basal ganglia, and cerebellum.
label: sentence

sentence: In addition to all of the above, the brain and spinal cord contain extensive circuitry to control the autonomic nervous system, which works by secreting hormones and by modulating the "smooth" muscles of the gut.

sentence: The autonomic nervous system affects heart rate, digestion, respiration rate, salivation, perspiration, urination, and sexual arousal, and several other processes.
label: sentence

sentence: Most of its functions are not under direct voluntary control.
label: sentence

sentence: A key component of the arousal system is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a tiny part of the hypothalamus located directly above the point at which the optic nerves from the two eyes cross.
label: sentence

sentence: The SCN contains the body's central biological clock.
label: sentence

sentence: Neurons there show activity levels that rise and fall with a period of about 24 hours, circadian rhythms: these activity fluctuations are driven by rhythmic changes in expression of a set of "clock genes".
label: sentence

sentence: The SCN continues to keep time even if it is excised from the brain and placed in a dish of warm nutrient solution, but it ordinarily receives input from the optic nerves, through the retinohypothalamic tract (RHT), that allows daily light-dark cycles to calibrate the clock.
label: sentence

sentence: The SCN projects to a set of areas in the hypothalamus, brainstem, and midbrain that are involved in implementing sleep-wake cycles.
label: sentence

sentence: An important component of the system is the reticular formation, a group of neuron-clusters scattered diffusely through the core of the lower brain.
label: sentence

sentence: Reticular neurons send signals to the thalamus, which in turn sends activity-level-controlling signals to every part of the cortex.

sentence: Damage to the reticular formation can produce a permanent state of coma.
label: sentence

sentence: Sleep involves great changes in brain activity.
label: sentence

sentence: Until the 1950s it was generally believed that the brain essentially shuts off during sleep, but this is now known to be far from true; activity continues, but patterns become very different.
label: sentence

sentence: There are two types of sleep: REM sleep (with dreaming) and NREM (non-REM, usually without dreaming) sleep, which repeat in slightly varying patterns throughout a sleep episode.
label: sentence

sentence: Three broad types of distinct brain activity patterns can be measured: REM, light NREM and deep NREM.
label: sentence

sentence: During deep NREM sleep, also called slow wave sleep, activity in the cortex takes the form of large synchronized waves, whereas in the waking state it is noisy and desynchronized.
label: sentence

sentence: Levels of the neurotransmitters norepinephrine and serotonin drop during slow wave sleep, and fall almost to zero during REM sleep; levels of acetylcholine show the reverse pattern.

sentence: For any animal, survival requires maintaining a variety of parameters of bodily state within a limited range of variation: these include temperature, water content, salt concentration in the bloodstream, blood glucose levels, blood oxygen level, and others.

sentence: The ability of an animal to regulate the internal environment of its body—the milieu intérieur, as pioneering physiologist Claude Bernard called it—is known as homeostasis (Greek for "standing still").
label: sentence

sentence: Maintaining homeostasis is a crucial function of the brain.
label: sentence

sentence: The basic principle that underlies homeostasis is negative feedback: any time a parameter diverges from its set-point, sensors generate an error signal that evokes a response that causes the parameter to shift back toward its optimum value.
label: sentence

sentence: (This principle is widely used in engineering, for example in the control of temperature using a thermostat.)

sentence: In vertebrates, the part of the brain that plays the greatest role is the hypothalamus, a small region at the base of the forebrain whose size does not reflect its complexity or the importance of its function.

sentence: Several hypothalamic nuclei receive input from sensors located in the lining of blood vessels, conveying information about temperature, sodium level, glucose level, blood oxygen level, and other parameters.

sentence: These hypothalamic nuclei send output signals to motor areas that can generate actions to rectify deficiencies.
label: sentence

sentence: Some of the outputs also go to the pituitary gland, a tiny gland attached to the brain directly underneath the hypothalamus.

sentence: The pituitary gland secretes hormones into the bloodstream, where they circulate throughout the body and induce changes in cellular activity.

sentence: Most organisms studied to date utilize a reward–punishment mechanism: for instance, worms and insects can alter their behavior to seek food sources or to avoid dangers.

sentence: In vertebrates, the reward-punishment system is implemented by a specific set of brain structures, at the heart of which lie the basal ganglia, a set of interconnected areas at the base of the forebrain.

sentence: There is substantial evidence that the basal ganglia are the central site at which decisions are made: the basal ganglia exert a sustained inhibitory control over most of the motor systems in the brain; when this inhibition is released, a motor system is permitted to execute the action it is programmed to carry out.

sentence: Rewards and punishments function by altering the relationship between the inputs that the basal ganglia receive and the decision-signals that are emitted.

sentence: The reward mechanism is better understood than the punishment mechanism, because its role in drug abuse has caused it to be studied very intensively.

sentence: Research has shown that the neurotransmitter dopamine plays a central role: addictive drugs such as cocaine, amphetamine, and nicotine either cause dopamine levels to rise or cause the effects of dopamine inside the brain to be enhanced.

sentence: Almost all animals are capable of modifying their behavior as a result of experience—even the most primitive types of worms.

sentence: Because behavior is driven by brain activity, changes in behavior must somehow correspond to changes inside the brain.

sentence: Until 1970, however, experimental evidence to support the synaptic plasticity hypothesis was lacking.

sentence: Since then technical advances have made these sorts of experiments much easier to carry out, and thousands of studies have been made that have clarified the mechanism of synaptic change, and uncovered other types of activity-driven synaptic change in a variety of brain areas, including the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, basal ganglia, and cerebellum.

sentence: The field of neuroscience encompasses all approaches that seek to understand the brain and the rest of the nervous system.

sentence: The brain is also the most important organ studied in psychiatry, the branch of medicine that works to study, prevent, and treat mental disorders.

sentence: The oldest method of studying the brain is anatomical, and until the middle of the 20th century, much of the progress in neuroscience came from the development of better cell stains and better microscopes.

sentence: Neuroanatomists study the large-scale structure of the brain as well as the microscopic structure of neurons and their components, especially synapses.

sentence: Among other tools, they employ a plethora of stains that reveal neural structure, chemistry, and connectivity.

sentence: In recent years, the development of immunostaining techniques has allowed investigation of neurons that express specific sets of genes.

sentence: Also, functional neuroanatomy uses medical imaging techniques to correlate variations in human brain structure with differences in cognition or behavior.

sentence: Neurophysiologists study the chemical, pharmacological, and electrical properties of the brain: their primary tools are drugs and recording devices.
label: sentence

sentence: Thousands of experimentally developed drugs affect the nervous system, some in highly specific ways.
label: sentence

sentence: Recordings of brain activity can be made using electrodes, either glued to the scalp as in EEG studies, or implanted inside the brains of animals for extracellular recordings, which can detect action potentials generated by individual neurons.
label: sentence

sentence: Because the brain does not contain pain receptors, it is possible using these techniques to record brain activity from animals that are awake and behaving without causing distress.
label: sentence

sentence: The same techniques have occasionally been used to study brain activity in human patients suffering from intractable epilepsy, in cases where there was a medical necessity to implant electrodes to localize the brain area responsible for epileptic seizures.
label: sentence

sentence: Functional imaging techniques such as functional magnetic resonance imaging are also used to study brain activity; these techniques have mainly been used with human subjects, because they require a conscious subject to remain motionless for long periods of time, but they have the great advantage of being noninvasive.

sentence: Another approach to brain function is to examine the consequences of damage to specific brain areas.
label: sentence

sentence: Even though it is protected by the skull and meninges, surrounded by cerebrospinal fluid, and isolated from the bloodstream by the blood–brain barrier, the delicate nature of the brain makes it vulnerable to numerous diseases and several types of damage.
label: sentence

sentence: In humans, the effects of strokes and other types of brain damage have been a key source of information about brain function.

sentence: Because there is no ability to experimentally control the nature of the damage, however, this information is often difficult to interpret.

sentence: In animal studies, most commonly involving rats, it is possible to use electrodes or locally injected chemicals to produce precise patterns of damage and then examine the consequences for behavior.

sentence: Computational neuroscience encompasses two approaches: first, the use of computers to study the brain; second, the study of how brains perform computation.
label: sentence

sentence: On one hand, it is possible to write a computer program to simulate the operation of a group of neurons by making use of systems of equations that describe their electrochemical activity; such simulations are known as biologically realistic neural networks.

sentence: On the other hand, it is possible to study algorithms for neural computation by simulating, or mathematically analyzing, the operations of simplified "units" that have some of the properties of neurons but abstract out much of their biological complexity.

sentence: The computational functions of the brain are studied both by computer scientists and neuroscientists.

sentence: Recent years have seen increasing applications of genetic and genomic techniques to the study of the brain  and a focus on the roles of neurotrophic factors and physical activity in neuroplasticity.

sentence: Phonology is a branch of linguistics concerned with the systematic organization of sounds in languages.

sentence: It has traditionally focused largely on the study of the systems of phonemes in particular languages (and therefore used to be also called phonemics, or phonematics), but it may also cover any linguistic analysis either at a level beneath the word (including syllable, onset and rime, articulatory gestures, articulatory features, mora, etc.)

sentence: Phonology also includes the study of equivalent organizational systems in sign languages.

sentence: The word phonology (as in the phonology of English) can also refer to the phonological system (sound system) of a given language.

sentence: This is one of the fundamental systems which a language is considered to comprise, like its syntax and its vocabulary.
label: sentence

sentence: Phonology is often distinguished from phonetics.
label: sentence

sentence: While phonetics concerns the physical production, acoustic transmission and perception of the sounds of speech, phonology describes the way sounds function within a given language or across languages to encode meaning.
label: sentence

sentence: For many linguists, phonetics belongs to descriptive linguistics, and phonology to theoretical linguistics, although establishing the phonological system of a language is necessarily an application of theoretical principles to analysis of phonetic evidence.

sentence: Note that this distinction was not always made, particularly before the development of the modern concept of the phoneme in the mid 20th century.

sentence: Some subfields of modern phonology have a crossover with phonetics in descriptive disciplines such as psycholinguistics and speech perception, resulting in specific areas like articulatory phonology or laboratory phonology.

sentence: The word phonology comes from the Greek φωνή, phōnḗ, "voice, sound," and the suffix -logy (which is from Greek λόγος, lógos, "word, speech, subject of discussion").

sentence: Definitions of the term vary.

sentence: Nikolai Trubetzkoy in Grundzüge der Phonologie (1939) defines phonology as "the study of sound pertaining to the system of language," as opposed to phonetics, which is "the study of sound pertaining to the act of speech" (the distinction between language and speech being basically Saussure's distinction between langue and parole).

sentence: A general purpose computer has four main components: the arithmetic logic unit (ALU), the control unit, the memory, and the input and output devices (collectively termed I/O).

sentence: A key component common to all CPUs is the program counter, a special memory cell (a register) that keeps track of which location in memory the next instruction is to be read from.

sentence: Immunology is a branch of biomedical science that covers the study of immune systems in all organisms.
label: sentence

sentence: It charts, measures, and contextualizes the: physiological functioning of the immune system in states of both health and diseases; malfunctions of the immune system in immunological disorders (such as autoimmune diseases, hypersensitivities, immune deficiency, and transplant rejection); the physical, chemical and physiological characteristics of the components of the immune system in vitro, in situ, and in vivo.
label: sentence

sentence: Immunology has applications in numerous disciplines of medicine, particularly in the fields of organ transplantation, oncology, virology, bacteriology, parasitology, psychiatry, and dermatology.
label: sentence

sentence: Prior to the designation of immunity from the etymological root immunis, which is Latin for "exempt"; early physicians characterized organs that would later be proven as essential components of the immune system.
label: sentence

sentence: The important lymphoid organs of the immune system are the thymus and bone marrow, and chief lymphatic tissues such as spleen, tonsils, lymph vessels, lymph nodes, adenoids, and liver.
label: sentence

sentence: When health conditions worsen to emergency status, portions of immune system organs including the thymus, spleen, bone marrow, lymph nodes and other lymphatic tissues can be surgically excised for examination while patients are still alive.
label: sentence

sentence: Many components of the immune system are typically cellular in nature and not associated with any specific organ; but rather are embedded or circulating in various tissues located throughout the body.
label: sentence

sentence: Classical immunology ties in with the fields of epidemiology and medicine.
label: sentence

sentence: It studies the relationship between the body systems, pathogens, and immunity.
label: sentence

sentence: The earliest written mention of immunity can be traced back to the plague of Athens in 430 BCE.
label: sentence

sentence: Thucydides noted that people who had recovered from a previous bout of the disease could nurse the sick without contracting the illness a second time.
label: sentence

sentence: Many other ancient societies have references to this phenomenon, but it was not until the 19th and 20th centuries before the concept developed into scientific theory.
label: sentence

sentence: The study of the molecular and cellular components that comprise the immune system, including their function and interaction, is the central science of immunology.
label: sentence

sentence: The immune system has been divided into a more primitive innate immune system and, in vertebrates, an acquired or adaptive immune system.
label: sentence

sentence: The latter is further divided into humoral (or antibody) and cell-mediated components.
label: sentence

sentence: The humoral (antibody) response is defined as the interaction between antibodies and antigens.
label: sentence

sentence: Antibodies are specific proteins released from a certain class of immune cells known as B lymphocytes, while antigens are defined as anything that elicits the generation of antibodies ("anti"body "gen"erators).
label: sentence

sentence: Immunology rests on an understanding of the properties of these two biological entities and the cellular response to both.
label: sentence

sentence: Immunological research continues to become more specialized, pursuing non-classical models of immunity and functions of cells, organs and systems not previously associated with the immune system (Yemeserach 2010).
label: sentence

sentence: Clinical immunology is the study of diseases caused by disorders of the immune system (failure, aberrant action, and malignant growth of the cellular elements of the system).
label: sentence

sentence: It also involves diseases of other systems, where immune reactions play a part in the pathology and clinical features.
label: sentence

sentence: Other immune system disorders include various hypersensitivities (such as in asthma and other allergies) that respond inappropriately to otherwise harmless compounds.
label: sentence

sentence: The most well-known disease that affects the immune system itself is AIDS, an immunodeficiency characterized by the suppression of CD4+ ("helper") T cells, dendritic cells and macrophages by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV).
label: sentence

sentence: The body’s capability to react to antigen depends on a person's age, antigen type, maternal factors and the area where the antigen is presented.
label: sentence

sentence: Neonates are said to be in a state of physiological immunodeficiency, because both their innate and adaptive immunological responses are greatly suppressed.
label: sentence

sentence: Once born, a child’s immune system responds favorably to protein antigens while not as well to glycoproteins and polysaccharides.
label: sentence

sentence: In fact, many of the infections acquired by neonates are caused by low virulence organisms like Staphylococcus and Pseudomonas.
label: sentence

sentence: In neonates, opsonic activity and the ability to activate the complement cascade is very limited.
label: sentence

sentence: For example, the mean level of C3 in a newborn is approximately 65% of that found in the adult.
label: sentence

sentence: Phagocytic activity is also greatly impaired in newborns.
label: sentence

sentence: This is due to lower opsonic activity, as well as diminished up-regulation of integrin and selectin receptors, which limit the ability of neutrophils to interact with adhesion molecules in the endothelium.
label: sentence

sentence: Their monocytes are slow and have a reduced ATP production, which also limits the newborn's phagocytic activity.
label: sentence

sentence: Although, the number of total lymphocytes is significantly higher than in adults, the cellular and humoral immunity is also impaired.
label: sentence

sentence: Antigen-presenting cells in newborns have a reduced capability to activate T cells.
label: sentence

sentence: Also, T cells of a newborn proliferate poorly and produce very small amounts of cytokines like IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-12, and IFN-g which limits their capacity to activate the humoral response as well as the phagocitic activity of macrophage.

sentence: B cells develop early during gestation but are not fully active.

sentence: Some IgA is provided by breast milk.

sentence: These passively-acquired antibodies can protect the newborn for up to 18 months, but their response is usually short-lived and of low affinity.

sentence: These antibodies can also produce a negative response.

sentence: If a child is exposed to the antibody for a particular antigen before being exposed to the antigen itself then the child will produce a dampened response.

sentence: Immunology is strongly experimental in everyday practice but is also characterized by an ongoing theoretical attitude.

sentence: The end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century saw a battle between "cellular" and "humoral" theories of immunity.

sentence: According to the cellular theory of immunity, represented in particular by Elie Metchnikoff, it was cells – more precisely, phagocytes – that were responsible for immune responses.
label: sentence

sentence: In contrast, the humoral theory of immunity, held by Robert Koch and Emil von Behring, among others, stated that the active immune agents were soluble components (molecules) found in the organism’s “humors” rather than its cells.

sentence: On the basis of CST, Burnet developed a theory of how an immune response is triggered according to the self/nonself distinction: "self" constituents (constituents of the body) do not trigger destructive immune responses, while "nonself" entities (e.g., pathogens, an allograft) trigger a destructive immune response.

sentence: MPEG-1 or MPEG-2 Audio Layer III, more commonly referred to as MP3, is an audio coding format for digital audio which uses a form of lossy data compression.
label: sentence

sentence: It is a common audio format for consumer audio streaming or storage, as well as a de facto standard of digital audio compression for the transfer and playback of music on most digital audio players.
label: sentence

sentence: The use of lossy compression is designed to greatly reduce the amount of data required to represent the audio recording and still sound like a faithful reproduction of the original uncompressed audio for most listeners.
label: sentence

sentence: An MP3 file that is created using the setting of 128 kbit/s will result in a file that is about 1/11 the size of the CD file created from the original audio source (44,100 samples per second × 16 bits per sample × 2 channels = 1,411,200 bit/s; MP3 compressed at 128 kbit/s: 128,000 bit/s [1 k = 1,000, not 1024, because it is a bit rate].
label: sentence

sentence: An MP3 file can also be constructed at higher or lower bit rates, with higher or lower resulting quality.
label: sentence

sentence: The compression works by reducing the accuracy of certain parts of a sound that are considered to be beyond the auditory resolution ability of most people.
label: sentence

sentence: This method is commonly referred to as perceptual coding.
label: sentence

sentence: It uses psychoacoustic models to discard or reduce precision of components less audible to human hearing, and then records the remaining information in an efficient manner.
label: sentence

sentence: MP3 was designed by the Moving Picture Experts Group (MPEG) as part of its MPEG-1 standard and later extended in the MPEG-2 standard.

sentence: MPEG-1 Audio (MPEG-1 Part 3), which included MPEG-1 Audio Layer I, II and III was approved as a committee draft of ISO/IEC standard in 1991, finalised in 1992 and published in 1993 (ISO/IEC 11172-3:1993).

sentence: The MP3 lossy audio data compression algorithm takes advantage of a perceptual limitation of human hearing called auditory masking.

sentence: Most decoders are "bitstream compliant", which means that the decompressed output that they produce from a given MP3 file will be the same, within a specified degree of rounding tolerance, as the output specified mathematically in the ISO/IEC high standard document (ISO/IEC 11172-3).

sentence: When performing lossy audio encoding, such as creating an MP3 file, there is a trade-off between the amount of space used and the sound quality of the result.
label: sentence

sentence: Typically, the creator is allowed to set a bit rate, which specifies how many kilobits the file may use per second of audio.
label: sentence

sentence: The higher the bit rate, the larger the compressed file will be, and, generally, the closer it will sound to the original file.
label: sentence

sentence: With too low a bit rate, compression artifacts (i.e., sounds that were not present in the original recording) may be audible in the reproduction.
label: sentence

sentence: Some audio is hard to compress because of its randomness and sharp attacks.
label: sentence

sentence: When this type of audio is compressed, artifacts such as ringing or pre-echo are usually heard.
label: sentence

sentence: A sample of applause compressed with a relatively low bit rate provides a good example of compression artifacts.
label: sentence

sentence: Besides the bit rate of an encoded piece of audio, the quality of MP3 files also depends on the quality of the encoder itself, and the difficulty of the signal being encoded.
label: sentence

sentence: As the MP3 standard allows quite a bit of freedom with encoding algorithms, different encoders may feature quite different quality, even with identical bit rates.
label: sentence

sentence: As an example, in a public listening test featuring two different MP3 encoders at about 128 kbit/s, one scored 3.66 on a 1–5 scale, while the other scored only 2.22.
label: sentence

sentence: The simplest type of MP3 file uses one bit rate for the entire file: this is known as Constant Bit Rate (CBR) encoding.
label: sentence

sentence: Using a constant bit rate makes encoding simpler and faster.
label: sentence

sentence: However, it is also possible to create files where the bit rate changes throughout the file.
label: sentence

sentence: These are known as Variable Bit Rate (VBR) files.
label: sentence

sentence: The idea behind this is that, in any piece of audio, some parts will be much easier to compress, such as silence or music containing only a few instruments, while others will be more difficult to compress.
label: sentence

sentence: So, the overall quality of the file may be increased by using a lower bit rate for the less complex passages and a higher one for the more complex parts.
label: sentence

sentence: With some encoders, it is possible to specify a given quality, and the encoder will vary the bit rate accordingly.
label: sentence

sentence: Users who know a particular "quality setting" that is transparent to their ears can use this value when encoding all of their music, and generally speaking not need to worry about performing personal listening tests on each piece of music to determine the correct bit rate.
label: sentence

sentence: Perceived quality can be influenced by listening environment (ambient noise), listener attention, and listener training and in most cases by listener audio equipment (such as sound cards, speakers and headphones).
label: sentence

sentence: Several bit rates are specified in the MPEG-1 Audio Layer III standard: 32, 40, 48, 56, 64, 80, 96, 112, 128, 160, 192, 224, 256 and 320 kbit/s, with available sampling frequencies of 32, 44.1 and 48 kHz.

sentence: [citation needed] Because of the Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem, frequency reproduction is always strictly less than half of the sampling frequency, and imperfect filters requires a larger margin for error (noise level versus sharpness of filter), so 8 kHz sampling rate limits the maximum frequency to 4 kHz, while 48 kHz maximum sampling rate limits an MP3 to 24 kHz sound reproduction.

sentence: Later more sophisticated MP3 encoders were able to use the bit reservoir to target an average bit rate selecting the encoding rate for each frame based on the complexity of the sound in that portion of the recording.

sentence: Layer III audio can also use a "bit reservoir", a partially full frame's ability to hold part of the next frame's audio data, allowing temporary changes in effective bitrate, even in a constant bitrate stream.

sentence: A "tag" in an audio file is a section of the file that contains metadata such as the title, artist, album, track number or other information about the file's contents.
label: sentence

sentence: The MP3 standards do not define tag formats for MP3 files, nor is there a standard container format that would support metadata and obviate the need for tags.
label: sentence

sentence: However, several de facto standards for tag formats exist.
label: sentence

sentence: As of 2010, the most widespread are ID3v1 and ID3v2, and the more recently introduced APEv2.
label: sentence

sentence: These tags are normally embedded at the beginning or end of MP3 files, separate from the actual MP3 frame data.
label: sentence

sentence: MP3 decoders either extract information from the tags, or just treat them as ignorable, non-MP3 junk data.
label: sentence

sentence: ReplayGain is a standard for measuring and storing the loudness of an MP3 file (audio normalization) in its metadata tag, enabling a ReplayGain-compliant player to automatically adjust the overall playback volume for each file.
label: sentence

sentence: MP3Gain may be used to reversibly modify files based on ReplayGain measurements so that adjusted playback can be achieved on players without ReplayGain capability.

sentence: The Enlightenment – known in French as the Siècle des Lumières, the Century of Enlightenment, and in German as the Aufklärung – was a philosophical movement which dominated the world of ideas in Europe in the 18th century.

sentence: During that year and the next, Uruguayan revolutionary José Gervasio Artigas united with others from Buenos Aires against Spain.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1811, the forces deployed by the Junta Grande of Buenos Aires and the gaucho forces led by Artigas started a siege of Montevideo, which had refused to obey the directives of the new authorities of the May Revolution.
label: sentence

sentence: The siege was lifted at the end of that year, when the military situation started deteriorating in the Upper Peru region.
label: sentence

sentence: The Spanish governor was expelled in 1814.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1816, Portugal invaded the recently liberated territory and in 1821, it was annexed to the Banda Oriental of Brazil.
label: sentence

sentence: Juan Antonio Lavalleja and his band called the Treinta y Tres Orientales ("Thirty-Three Orientals") re-established the independence of the region in 1825.
label: sentence

sentence: Uruguay was consolidated as an independent state in 1828, with Montevideo as the nation's capital.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1829, the demolition of the city's fortifications began and plans were made for an extension beyond the Ciudad Vieja, referred to as the "Ciudad Nueva" ("new city").
label: sentence

sentence: Urban expansion, however, moved very slowly because of the events that followed.
label: sentence

sentence: Uruguay's 1830s were dominated by the confrontation between Manuel Oribe and Fructuoso Rivera, the two revolutionary leaders who had fought against the Empire of Brazil under the command of Lavalleja, each of whom had become the caudillo of their respective faction.
label: sentence

sentence: Politics were divided between Oribe's Blancos ("whites"), represented by the National Party, and Rivera's Colorados ("reds"), represented by the Colorado Party, with each party's name taken from the colour of its emblems.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1838, Oribe was forced to resign the presidency; he established a rebel army and began a long civil war, the Guerra Grande, which lasted until 1851.
label: sentence

sentence: The city of Montevideo suffered a siege of eight years between 1843 and 1851, during which it was supplied by sea with British and French support.
label: sentence

sentence: Oribe, with the support of the then conservative Governor of Buenos Aires Province Juan Manuel de Rosas, besieged the Colorados in Montevideo, where the latter were supported by the French Legion, the Italian Legion, the Basque Legion and battalions from Brazil.
label: sentence

sentence: Finally, in 1851, with the additional support of Argentine rebels who opposed Rosas, the Colorados defeated Oribe.
label: sentence

sentence: The fighting, however, resumed in 1855, when the Blancos came to power, which they maintained until 1865.
label: sentence

sentence: Thereafter, the Colorado Party regained power, which they retained until past the middle of the 20th century.
label: sentence

sentence: After the end of hostilities, a period of growth and expansion started for the city.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1853 a stagecoach bus line was established joining Montevideo with the newly formed settlement of Unión and the first natural gas street lights were inaugurated.
label: sentence

sentence: [citation needed] From 1854 to 1861 the first public sanitation facilities were constructed.

sentence: In 1856 the Teatro Solís was inaugurated, 15 years after the beginning of its construction.
label: sentence

sentence: By Decree, on December 1861 the areas of Aguada and Cordón were incorporated to the growing Ciudad Nueva (New City).
label: sentence

sentence: In 1866, an underwater telegraph line connected the city with Buenos Aires.
label: sentence

sentence: The statue of Peace, La Paz, was erected on a column in Plaza Cagancha and the building of the Postal Service as well as the bridge of Paso Molino were inaugurated in 1867.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1868, the horse-drawn tram company Compañía de Tranvías al Paso del Molino y Cerro created the first lines connecting Montevideo with Unión, the beach resort of Capurro and the industrialized and economically independent Villa del Cerro, at the time called Cosmopolis.
label: sentence

sentence: In the same year, the Mercado del Puerto was inaugurated.

sentence: During the same year and the next, the neighbourhoods Colón, Nuevo París and La Comercial were founded.

sentence: By Decree, on 8 January 1881, the area Los Pocitos was incorporated to the Novísima Ciudad (Most New City).

sentence: The first telephone lines were installed in 1882 and electric street lights took the place of the gas operated ones in 1886.

sentence: The Hipódromo de Maroñas started operating in 1888, and the neighbourhoods of Reus del Sur, Reus del Norte and Conciliación were inaugurated in 1889.

sentence: During World War II, a famous incident involving the German pocket battleship Admiral Graf Spee took place in Punta del Este, 200 kilometers (120 mi) from Montevideo.

sentence: Montevideo is situated on the north shore of the Río de la Plata, the arm of the Atlantic Ocean that separates the south coast of Uruguay from the north coast of Argentina; Buenos Aires lies 230 kilometres (140 mi) west on the Argentine side.

sentence: The Santa Lucía River forms a natural border between Montevideo and San José Department to its west.
label: sentence

sentence: To the city's north and east is Canelones Department, with the stream of Carrasco forming the eastern natural border.
label: sentence

sentence: The coastline forming the city's southern border is interspersed with rocky protrusions and sandy beaches.
label: sentence

sentence: The Bay of Montevideo forms a natural harbour, the nation's largest and one of the largest in the Southern Cone, and the finest natural port in the region, functioning as a crucial component of the Uruguayan economy and foreign trade.
label: sentence

sentence: Various streams criss-cross the town and empty into the Bay of Montevideo.
label: sentence

sentence: The coastline and rivers are heavily polluted and of high salinity.
label: sentence

sentence: The city has an average elevation of 43 metres (141 ft).
label: sentence

sentence: Its highest elevations are two hills: the Cerro de Montevideo and the Cerro de la Victoria, with the highest point, the peak of Cerro de Montevideo, crowned by a fortress, the Fortaleza del Cerro at a height of 134 metres (440 ft).

sentence: Closest cities by road are Las Piedras to the north and the so-called Ciudad de la Costa (a conglomeration of coastal towns) to the east, both in the range of 20 to 25 kilometres (16 mi) from the city center.
label: sentence

sentence: The approximate distances to the neighbouring department capitals by road are, 90 kilometres (56 mi) to San Jose de Mayo (San Jose Department) and 46 kilometres (29 mi) to Canelones (Canelones Department).

sentence: The Municipality of Montevideo was first created by a legal act of 18 December 1908.
label: sentence

sentence: The municipality's first mayor (1909–1911) was Daniel Muñoz.
label: sentence

sentence: Municipalities were abolished by the Uruguayan Constitution of 1918, effectively restored during the 1933 military coup of Gabriel Terra, and formally restored by the 1934 Constitution.
label: sentence

sentence: The 1952 Constitution again decided to abolish the municipalities; it came into effect in February 1955.
label: sentence

sentence: Municipalities were replaced by departmental councils, which consisted of a collegiate executive board with 7 members from Montevideo and 5 from the interior region.
label: sentence

sentence: However, municipalities were revived under the 1967 Constitution and have operated continuously since that time.
label: sentence

sentence: As of 2010[update], the city of Montevideo has been divided into 8 political municipalities (Municipios), referred to with the letters from A to G, including CH, each presided over by a mayor elected by the citizens registered in the constituency.
label: sentence

sentence: This division, according to the Municipality of Montevideo, "aims to advance political and administrative decentralization in the department of Montevideo, with the aim of deepening the democratic participation of citizens in governance."
label: sentence

sentence: The head of each Municipio is called an alcalde or (if female) alcaldesa.
label: sentence

sentence: Of much greater importance is the division of the city into 62 barrios: neighbourhoods or wards.
label: sentence

sentence: Many of the city's barrios—such as Sayago, Ituzaingó and Pocitos—were previously geographically separate settlements, later absorbed by the growth of the city.
label: sentence

sentence: Others grew up around certain industrial sites, including the salt-curing works of Villa del Cerro and the tanneries in Nuevo París.
label: sentence

sentence: Each barrio has its own identity, geographic location and socio-cultural activities.
label: sentence

sentence: A neighbourhood of great significance is Ciudad Vieja, that was surrounded by a protective wall until 1829.
label: sentence

sentence: This area contains most important buildings of the colonial era and early decades of independence.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1860, Montevideo had 57,913 inhabitants including a number of people of African origin who had been brought as slaves and had gained their freedom around the middle of the century.
label: sentence

sentence: By 1880, the population had quadrupled, mainly because of the great European immigration.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1908, its population had grown massively to 309,331 inhabitants.
label: sentence

sentence: In the course of the 20th century the city continued to receive large numbers of European immigrants, especially Spanish and Italian, followed by French, Germans or Dutch, English or Irish, Polish, Greek, Hungarians, Russians, Croats, Lebanese, Armenians, and Jews of various origins.
label: sentence

sentence: The last wave of immigrants occurred between 1945 and 1955.

sentence: According to the census survey carried out between 15 June and 31 July 2004, Montevideo had a population of 1,325,968 persons, compared to Uruguay's total population of 3,241,003.
label: sentence

sentence: The female population was 707,697 (53.4%) while the male population accounted for 618,271 (46.6%).
label: sentence

sentence: The population had declined since the previous census carried out in 1996, with an average annual growth rate of −1.5 per thousand.
label: sentence

sentence: Continual decline has been documented since the census period of 1975–1985, which showed a rate of −5.6 per thousand.
label: sentence

sentence: The decrease is due in large part to lowered fertility, partly offset by mortality, and to a smaller degree in migration.
label: sentence

sentence: The birth rate declined by 19% from 1996 (17 per thousand) to 2004 (13.8 per thousand).
label: sentence

sentence: Similarly, the total fertility rate (TFR) declined from 2.24 in 1996 to 1.79 in 2004.

sentence: However, mortality continued to fall with life expectancy at birth for both sexes increasing by 1.73 years.

sentence: As the capital of Uruguay, Montevideo is the economic and political centre of the country.
label: sentence

sentence: Most of the largest and wealthiest businesses in Uruguay have their headquarters in the city.
label: sentence

sentence: Since the 1990s the city has undergone rapid economic development and modernization, including two of Uruguay's most important buildings—the World Trade Center Montevideo (1998), and Telecommunications Tower (2000), the headquarters of Uruguay's government-owned telecommunications company ANTEL, increasing the city's integration into the global marketplace.
label: sentence

sentence: The most important state-owned companies headquartered in Montevideo are: AFE (railways), ANCAP (Energy), Administracion Nacional de Puertos (Ports), ANTEL (telecommunications), BHU (savings and loan), BROU (bank), BSE (insurance), OSE (water & sewage), UTE (electricity).
label: sentence

sentence: These companies operate under public law, using a legal entity defined in the Uruguayan Constitution called Ente Autonomo ("autonomous entity").

sentence: Banking has traditionally been one of the strongest service export sectors in Uruguay: the country was once dubbed "the Switzerland of America", mainly for its banking sector and stability, although that stability has been threatened in the 21st century by the recent global economic climate.

sentence: The largest bank in Uruguay is Banco Republica (BROU), based in Montevideo.

sentence: There are also a myriad of brokers and financial-services bureaus, among them Ficus Capital, Galfin Sociedad de Bolsa, Europa Sociedad de Bolsa, Darío Cukier, GBU, Hordeñana & Asociados Sociedad de Bolsa, etc.

sentence: Tourism accounts for much of Uruguay's economy.
label: sentence

sentence: Tourism in Montevideo is centered in the Ciudad Vieja area, which includes the city's oldest buildings, several museums, art galleries, and nightclubs, with Sarandí Street and the Mercado del Puerto being the most frequented venues of the old city.

sentence: On the edge of Ciudad Vieja, Plaza Independencia is surrounded by many sights, including the Solís Theatre and the Palacio Salvo; the plaza also constitutes one end of 18 de Julio Avenue, the city's most important tourist destination outside of Ciudad Vieja.

sentence: Apart from being a shopping street, the avenue is noted for its Art Deco buildings, three important public squares, the Gaucho Museum, the Palacio Municipal and many other sights.

sentence: The avenue leads to the Obelisk of Montevideo; beyond that is Parque Batlle, which along with the Parque Prado is another important tourist destination.

sentence: Along the coast, the Fortaleza del Cerro, the Rambla (the coastal avenue), 13 kilometres (8.1 mi) of sandy beaches, and Punta Gorda attract many tourists, as do the Barrio Sur and Palermo barrios.

sentence: Montevideo has over 50 hotels, mostly located within the downtown area or along the beachfront of the Rambla de Montevideo.

sentence: Many of the hotels are in the modern, western style, such as the Sheraton Montevideo, the Radisson Montevideo Victoria Plaza Hotel located on the central Plaza Independencia, and the Plaza Fuerte Hotel on the waterfront.

sentence: Montevideo is the heartland of retailing in Uruguay.

sentence: The city has become the principal centre of business and real estate, including many expensive buildings and modern towers for residences and offices, surrounded by extensive green spaces.

sentence: In 1985, the first shopping centre in Rio de la Plata, Montevideo Shopping was built.

sentence: In 1994, with building of three more shopping complexes such as the Shopping Tres Cruces, Portones Shopping, and Punta Carretas Shopping, the business map of the city changed dramatically.

sentence: Global firms such as McDonald's and Burger King etc.

sentence: are firmly established in Montevideo.

sentence: The architecture of Montevideo ranges from Neoclassical buildings such as the Montevideo Metropolitan Cathedral to the Postmodern style of the World Trade Center Montevideo or the 158-metre (518 ft) ANTEL Telecommunication Tower, the tallest skyscraper in the country.

sentence: The Along with the Telecommunications Tower, the Palacio Salvo dominates the skyline of the Bay of Montevideo.

sentence: The building façades in the Old Town reflect the city's extensive European immigration, displaying the influence of old European architecture.

sentence: Notable government buildings include the Legislative Palace, the City Hall, Estévez Palace and the Executive Tower.

sentence: The most notable sports stadium is the Estadio Centenario within Parque Batlle.

sentence: Parque Batlle, Parque Rodó and Parque Prado are Montevideo's three great parks.

sentence: Other landmarks in Pocitos are the "Edificio Panamericano" designed by Raul Sichero, and the "Positano" and "El Pilar" designed by Adolfo Sommer Smith and Luis García Pardo in the 1950s and 1960s.

sentence: However, the construction boom of the 1970s and 1980s transformed the face of this neighbourhood, with a cluster of modern apartment buildings for upper and upper middle class residents.

sentence: The current barrio of Parque Battle includes four former districts: Belgrano, Italiano, Villa Dolores and Batlle Park itself and borders the neighbourhoods of La Blanqueada, Tres Cruces, Pocitos and Buceo.

sentence: It has a high population density and most of its households are of medium-high- or high-income.

sentence: On their grounds, they started a private collection of animals that became a zoological garden and was passed to the city in 1919; in 1955 the Planetarium of Montevideo was built within its premises.

sentence: In an ecosystem, predation is a biological interaction where a predator (an organism that is hunting) feeds on its prey (the organism that is attacked).
label: sentence

sentence: Predators may or may not kill their prey prior to feeding on them, but the act of predation often results in the death of the prey and the eventual absorption of the prey's tissue through consumption.
label: sentence

sentence: Thus predation is often, though not always, carnivory.
label: sentence

sentence: Other categories of consumption are herbivory (eating parts of plants), fungivory (eating parts of fungi), and detritivory (the consumption of dead organic material (detritus)).
label: sentence

sentence: All these consumption categories fall under the rubric of consumer-resource systems.
label: sentence

sentence: It can often be difficult to separate various types of feeding behaviors.
label: sentence

sentence: For example, some parasitic species prey on a host organism and then lay their eggs on it for their offspring to feed on it while it continues to live in or on its decaying corpse after it has died.
label: sentence

sentence: The key characteristic of predation however is the predator's direct impact on the prey population.
label: sentence

sentence: On the other hand, detritivores simply eat dead organic material arising from the decay of dead individuals and have no direct impact on the "donor" organism(s).
label: sentence

sentence: Classification of predators by the extent to which they feed on and interact with their prey is one way ecologists may wish to categorize the different types of predation.
label: sentence

sentence: Instead of focusing on what they eat, this system classifies predators by the way in which they eat, and the general nature of the interaction between predator and prey species.
label: sentence

sentence: Two factors are considered here: How close the predator and prey are (in the latter two cases the term prey may be replaced with host) and whether or not the prey are directly murdered by the predator is considered, with true predation and parasitoidism involving certain death.
label: sentence

sentence: A true predator can commonly be known as one that kills and eats another living thing.
label: sentence

sentence: Whereas other types of predator all harm their prey in some way, this form kills them.
label: sentence

sentence: Predators may hunt actively for prey in pursuit predation, or sit and wait for prey to approach within striking distance, as in ambush predators.
label: sentence

sentence: Some predators kill large prey and dismember or chew it prior to eating it, such as a jaguar or a human; others may eat their (usually much smaller) prey whole, as does a bottlenose dolphin swallowing a fish, or a snake, duck or stork swallowing a frog.
label: sentence

sentence: Some animals that kill both large and small prey for their size (domestic cats and dogs are prime examples) may do either depending upon the circumstances; either would devour a large insect whole but dismember a rabbit.
label: sentence

sentence: Some predation entails venom that subdues a prey creature before the predator ingests the prey by killing, which the box jellyfish does, or disabling it, found in the behavior of the cone shell.
label: sentence

sentence: In some cases, the venom, as in rattlesnakes and some spiders, contributes to the digestion of the prey item even before the predator begins eating.
label: sentence

sentence: In other cases, the prey organism may die in the mouth or digestive system of the predator.
label: sentence

sentence: Baleen whales, for example, eat millions of microscopic plankton at once, the prey being broken down well after entering the whale.
label: sentence

sentence: Seed predation and egg predation are other forms of true predation, as seeds and eggs represent potential organisms.
label: sentence

sentence: Predators of this classification need not eat prey entirely.
label: sentence

sentence: For example, some predators cannot digest bones, while others can.
label: sentence

sentence: Some may eat only part of an organism, as in grazing (see below), but still consistently cause its direct death.
label: sentence

sentence: Grazing organisms may also kill their prey species, but this is seldom the case.
label: sentence

sentence: While some herbivores like zooplankton live on unicellular phytoplankton and therefore, by the individualized nature of the organism, kill their prey, many only eat a small part of the plant.
label: sentence

sentence: Grazing livestock may pull some grass out at the roots, but most is simply grazed upon, allowing the plant to regrow once again.
label: sentence

sentence: Kelp is frequently grazed in subtidal kelp forests, but regrows at the base of the blade continuously to cope with browsing pressure.
label: sentence

sentence: Animals may also be 'grazed' upon; female mosquitos land on hosts briefly to gain sufficient proteins for the development of their offspring.
label: sentence

sentence: Starfish may be grazed on, being capable of regenerating lost arms.
label: sentence

sentence: Parasites can at times be difficult to distinguish from grazers.
label: sentence

sentence: Their feeding behavior is similar in many ways, however they are noted for their close association with their host species.
label: sentence

sentence: While a grazing species such as an elephant may travel many kilometers in a single day, grazing on many plants in the process, parasites form very close associations with their hosts, usually having only one or at most a few in their lifetime.
label: sentence

sentence: This close living arrangement may be described by the term symbiosis, "living together", but unlike mutualism the association significantly reduces the fitness of the host.
label: sentence

sentence: Parasitic organisms range from the macroscopic mistletoe, a parasitic plant, to microscopic internal parasites such as cholera.
label: sentence

sentence: Some species however have more loose associations with their hosts.
label: sentence

sentence: Lepidoptera (butterfly and moth) larvae may feed parasitically on only a single plant, or they may graze on several nearby plants.
label: sentence

sentence: It is therefore wise to treat this classification system as a continuum rather than four isolated forms.
label: sentence

sentence: Parasitoids are organisms living in or on their host and feeding directly upon it, eventually leading to its death.
label: sentence

sentence: They are much like parasites in their close symbiotic relationship with their host or hosts.
label: sentence

sentence: Like the previous two classifications parasitoid predators do not kill their hosts instantly.
label: sentence

sentence: However, unlike parasites, they are very similar to true predators in that the fate of their prey is quite inevitably death.
label: sentence

sentence: A well-known example of a parasitoids are the ichneumon wasps, solitary insects living a free life as an adult, then laying eggs on or in another species such as a caterpillar.
label: sentence

sentence: Its larva(e) feed on the growing host causing it little harm at first, but soon devouring the internal organs until finally destroying the nervous system resulting in prey death.
label: sentence

sentence: By this stage the young wasp(s) are developed sufficiently to move to the next stage in their life cycle.
label: sentence

sentence: Though limited mainly to the insect order Hymenoptera, Diptera and Coleoptera parasitoids make up as much as 10% of all insect species.

sentence: Among predators there is a large degree of specialization.
label: sentence

sentence: Many predators specialize in hunting only one species of prey.
label: sentence

sentence: Others are more opportunistic and will kill and eat almost anything (examples: humans, leopards, dogs and alligators).
label: sentence

sentence: The specialists are usually particularly well suited to capturing their preferred prey.
label: sentence

sentence: The prey in turn, are often equally suited to escape that predator.
label: sentence

sentence: This is called an evolutionary arms race and tends to keep the populations of both species in equilibrium.
label: sentence

sentence: Some predators specialize in certain classes of prey, not just single species.
label: sentence

sentence: Some will switch to other prey (with varying degrees of success) when the preferred target is extremely scarce, and they may also resort to scavenging or a herbivorous diet if possible.

sentence: One way of classifying predators is by trophic level.

sentence: Organisms that feed on autotrophs, the producers of the trophic pyramid, are known as herbivores or primary consumers; those that feed on heterotrophs such as animals are known as secondary consumers.

sentence: A predator at the top of any food chain (that is, one that is preyed upon by no organism) is called an apex predator; examples include the orca, sperm whale, anaconda, Komodo dragon, tiger, lion, tiger shark, Nile crocodile, and most eagles and owls—and even omnivorous humans and grizzly bears.
