sentence: By the 1st century BC, negative numbers and decimal fractions were in use and The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art included methods for extracting higher order roots by Horner's method and solving linear equations and by Pythagoras' theorem.
label: sentence

sentence: Cubic equations were solved in the Tang dynasty and solutions of equations of order higher than 3 appeared in print in 1245 AD by Ch'in Chiu-shao.
label: sentence

sentence: Pascal's triangle for binomial coefficients was described around 1100 by Jia Xian.
label: sentence

sentence: Astronomy: Astronomical observations from China constitute the longest continuous sequence from any civilisation and include records of sunspots (112 records from 364 BC), supernovas (1054), lunar and solar eclipses.
label: sentence

sentence: By the 12th century, they could reasonably accurately make predictions of eclipses, but the knowledge of this was lost during the Ming dynasty, so that the Jesuit Matteo Ricci gained much favour in 1601 by his predictions.
label: sentence

sentence: By 635 Chinese astronomers had observed that the tails of comets always point away from the sun.
label: sentence

sentence: Seismology: To better prepare for calamities, Zhang Heng invented a seismometer in 132 CE which provided instant alert to authorities in the capital Luoyang that an earthquake had occurred in a location indicated by a specific cardinal or ordinal direction.
label: sentence

sentence: Although no tremors could be felt in the capital when Zhang told the court that an earthquake had just occurred in the northwest, a message came soon afterwards that an earthquake had indeed struck 400 km (248 mi) to 500 km (310 mi) northwest of Luoyang (in what is now modern Gansu).
label: sentence

sentence: Zhang called his device the 'instrument for measuring the seasonal winds and the movements of the Earth' (Houfeng didong yi 候风地动仪), so-named because he and others thought that earthquakes were most likely caused by the enormous compression of trapped air.
label: sentence

sentence: See Zhang's seismometer for further details.
label: sentence

sentence: There are many notable contributors to the field of Chinese science throughout the ages.
label: sentence

sentence: One of the best examples would be Shen Kuo (1031–1095), a polymath scientist and statesman who was the first to describe the magnetic-needle compass used for navigation, discovered the concept of true north, improved the design of the astronomical gnomon, armillary sphere, sight tube, and clepsydra, and described the use of drydocks to repair boats.
label: sentence

sentence: After observing the natural process of the inundation of silt and the find of marine fossils in the Taihang Mountains (hundreds of miles from the Pacific Ocean), Shen Kuo devised a theory of land formation, or geomorphology.
label: sentence

sentence: He also adopted a theory of gradual climate change in regions over time, after observing petrified bamboo found underground at Yan'an, Shaanxi province.
label: sentence

sentence: If not for Shen Kuo's writing, the architectural works of Yu Hao would be little known, along with the inventor of movable type printing, Bi Sheng (990-1051).
label: sentence

sentence: Shen's contemporary Su Song (1020–1101) was also a brilliant polymath, an astronomer who created a celestial atlas of star maps, wrote a pharmaceutical treatise with related subjects of botany, zoology, mineralogy, and metallurgy, and had erected a large astronomical clocktower in Kaifeng city in 1088.
label: sentence

sentence: To operate the crowning armillary sphere, his clocktower featured an escapement mechanism and the world's oldest known use of an endless power-transmitting chain drive.
label: sentence

sentence: The Jesuit China missions of the 16th and 17th centuries "learned to appreciate the scientific achievements of this ancient culture and made them known in Europe.
label: sentence

sentence: Through their correspondence European scientists first learned about the Chinese science and culture."
label: sentence

sentence: Western academic thought on the history of Chinese technology and science was galvanized by the work of Joseph Needham and the Needham Research Institute.
label: sentence

sentence: Among the technological accomplishments of China were, according to the British scholar Needham, early seismological detectors (Zhang Heng in the 2nd century), the water-powered celestial globe (Zhang Heng), matches, the independent invention of the decimal system, dry docks, sliding calipers, the double-action piston pump, cast iron, the blast furnace, the iron plough, the multi-tube seed drill, the wheelbarrow, the suspension bridge, the winnowing machine, the rotary fan, the parachute, natural gas as fuel, the raised-relief map, the propeller, the crossbow, and a solid fuel rocket, the multistage rocket, the horse collar, along with contributions in logic, astronomy, medicine, and other fields.
label: sentence

sentence: With the division of the Roman Empire, the Western Roman Empire lost contact with much of its past.
label: sentence

sentence: In the Middle East, Greek philosophy was able to find some support under the newly created Arab Empire.
label: sentence

sentence: With the spread of Islam in the 7th and 8th centuries, a period of Muslim scholarship, known as the Islamic Golden Age, lasted until the 13th century.
label: sentence

sentence: This scholarship was aided by several factors.
label: sentence

sentence: The use of a single language, Arabic, allowed communication without need of a translator.
label: sentence

sentence: Access to Greek texts from the Byzantine Empire, along with Indian sources of learning, provided Muslim scholars a knowledge base to build upon.
label: sentence

sentence: Muslim scientists placed far greater emphasis on experiment than had the Greeks.
label: sentence

sentence: This led to an early scientific method being developed in the Muslim world, where significant progress in methodology was made, beginning with the experiments of Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) on optics from c. 1000, in his Book of Optics.
label: sentence

sentence: The law of refraction of light was known to the Persians.
label: sentence

sentence: The most important development of the scientific method was the use of experiments to distinguish between competing scientific theories set within a generally empirical orientation, which began among Muslim scientists.
label: sentence

sentence: Ibn al-Haytham is also regarded as the father of optics, especially for his empirical proof of the intromission theory of light.
label: sentence

sentence: Some have also described Ibn al-Haytham as the "first scientist" for his development of the modern scientific method.
label: sentence

sentence: In mathematics, the Persian mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi gave his name to the concept of the algorithm, while the term algebra is derived from al-jabr, the beginning of the title of one of his publications.
label: sentence

sentence: What is now known as Arabic numerals originally came from India, but Muslim mathematicians did make several refinements to the number system, such as the introduction of decimal point notation.
label: sentence

sentence: Sabian mathematician Al-Battani (850-929) contributed to astronomy and mathematics, while Persian scholar Al-Razi contributed to chemistry and medicine.
label: sentence

sentence: In astronomy, Al-Battani improved the measurements of Hipparchus, preserved in the translation of Ptolemy's Hè Megalè Syntaxis (The great treatise) translated as Almagest.
label: sentence

sentence: Al-Battani also improved the precision of the measurement of the precession of the Earth's axis.
label: sentence

sentence: The corrections made to the geocentric model by al-Battani, Ibn al-Haytham, Averroes and the Maragha astronomers such as Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, Mo'ayyeduddin Urdi and Ibn al-Shatir are similar to Copernican heliocentric model.
label: sentence

sentence: Heliocentric theories may have also been discussed by several other Muslim astronomers such as Ja'far ibn Muhammad Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi, Abu-Rayhan Biruni, Abu Said al-Sijzi, Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi, and Najm al-Dīn al-Qazwīnī al-Kātibī.
label: sentence

sentence: Ibn Sina (Avicenna) is regarded as the most influential philosopher of Islam.
label: sentence

sentence: He pioneered the science of experimental medicine and was the first physician to conduct clinical trials.
label: sentence

sentence: His two most notable works in medicine are the Kitāb al-shifāʾ ("Book of Healing") and The Canon of Medicine, both of which were used as standard medicinal texts in both the Muslim world and in Europe well into the 17th century.
label: sentence

sentence: Amongst his many contributions are the discovery of the contagious nature of infectious diseases, and the introduction of clinical pharmacology.
label: sentence

sentence: An intellectual revitalization of Europe started with the birth of medieval universities in the 12th century.
label: sentence

sentence: The contact with the Islamic world in Spain and Sicily, and during the Reconquista and the Crusades, allowed Europeans access to scientific Greek and Arabic texts, including the works of Aristotle, Ptolemy, Jābir ibn Hayyān, al-Khwarizmi, Alhazen, Avicenna, and Averroes.
label: sentence

sentence: European scholars had access to the translation programs of Raymond of Toledo, who sponsored the 12th century Toledo School of Translators from Arabic to Latin.
label: sentence

sentence: Later translators like Michael Scotus would learn Arabic in order to study these texts directly.
label: sentence

sentence: The European universities aided materially in the translation and propagation of these texts and started a new infrastructure which was needed for scientific communities.
label: sentence

sentence: In fact, European university put many works about the natural world and the study of nature at the center of its curriculum, with the result that the "medieval university laid far greater emphasis on science than does its modern counterpart and descendent."
label: sentence

sentence: At the beginning of the 13th century, there were reasonably accurate Latin translations of the main works of almost all the intellectually crucial ancient authors, allowing a sound transfer of scientific ideas via both the universities and the monasteries.
label: sentence

sentence: By then, the natural philosophy contained in these texts began to be extended by notable scholastics such as Robert Grosseteste, Roger Bacon, Albertus Magnus and Duns Scotus.
label: sentence

sentence: Precursors of the modern scientific method, influenced by earlier contributions of the Islamic world, can be seen already in Grosseteste's emphasis on mathematics as a way to understand nature, and in the empirical approach admired by Bacon, particularly in his Opus Majus.
label: sentence

sentence: Pierre Duhem's provocative thesis of the Catholic Church's Condemnation of 1277 led to the study of medieval science as a serious discipline, "but no one in the field any longer endorses his view that modern science started in 1277".
label: sentence

sentence: However, many scholars agree with Duhem's view that the Middle Ages were a period of important scientific developments.
label: sentence

sentence: The first half of the 14th century saw much important scientific work being done, largely within the framework of scholastic commentaries on Aristotle's scientific writings.
label: sentence

sentence: William of Ockham introduced the principle of parsimony: natural philosophers should not postulate unnecessary entities, so that motion is not a distinct thing but is only the moving object and an intermediary "sensible species" is not needed to transmit an image of an object to the eye.
label: sentence

sentence: Scholars such as Jean Buridan and Nicole Oresme started to reinterpret elements of Aristotle's mechanics.
label: sentence

sentence: In particular, Buridan developed the theory that impetus was the cause of the motion of projectiles, which was a first step towards the modern concept of inertia.
label: sentence

sentence: The Oxford Calculators began to mathematically analyze the kinematics of motion, making this analysis without considering the causes of motion.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1348, the Black Death and other disasters sealed a sudden end to the previous period of massive philosophic and scientific development.
label: sentence

sentence: Yet, the rediscovery of ancient texts was improved after the Fall of Constantinople in 1453, when many Byzantine scholars had to seek refuge in the West.
label: sentence

sentence: Meanwhile, the introduction of printing was to have great effect on European society.
label: sentence

sentence: The facilitated dissemination of the printed word democratized learning and allowed a faster propagation of new ideas.
label: sentence

sentence: New ideas also helped to influence the development of European science at this point: not least the introduction of Algebra.
label: sentence

sentence: These developments paved the way for the Scientific Revolution, which may also be understood as a resumption of the process of scientific inquiry, halted at the start of the Black Death.
label: sentence

sentence: The renewal of learning in Europe, that began with 12th century Scholasticism, came to an end about the time of the Black Death, and the initial period of the subsequent Italian Renaissance is sometimes seen as a lull in scientific activity.
label: sentence

sentence: The Northern Renaissance, on the other hand, showed a decisive shift in focus from Aristoteleian natural philosophy to chemistry and the biological sciences (botany, anatomy, and medicine).
label: sentence

sentence: Thus modern science in Europe was resumed in a period of great upheaval: the Protestant Reformation and Catholic Counter-Reformation; the discovery of the Americas by Christopher Columbus; the Fall of Constantinople; but also the re-discovery of Aristotle during the Scholastic period presaged large social and political changes.
label: sentence

sentence: Thus, a suitable environment was created in which it became possible to question scientific doctrine, in much the same way that Martin Luther and John Calvin questioned religious doctrine.
label: sentence

sentence: The works of Ptolemy (astronomy) and Galen (medicine) were found not always to match everyday observations.
label: sentence

sentence: Work by Vesalius on human cadavers found problems with the Galenic view of anatomy.
label: sentence

sentence: The willingness to question previously held truths and search for new answers resulted in a period of major scientific advancements, now known as the Scientific Revolution.
label: sentence

sentence: The Scientific Revolution is traditionally held by most historians to have begun in 1543, when the books De humani corporis fabrica (On the Workings of the Human Body) by Andreas Vesalius, and also De Revolutionibus, by the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, were first printed.
label: sentence

sentence: The thesis of Copernicus' book was that the Earth moved around the Sun.
label: sentence

sentence: The period culminated with the publication of the Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica in 1687 by Isaac Newton, representative of the unprecedented growth of scientific publications throughout Europe.
label: sentence

sentence: The Age of Enlightenment was a European affair.
label: sentence

sentence: The 17th century "Age of Reason" opened the avenues to the decisive steps towards modern science, which took place during the 18th century "Age of Enlightenment".
label: sentence

sentence: Directly based on the works of Newton, Descartes, Pascal and Leibniz, the way was now clear to the development of modern mathematics, physics and technology by the generation of Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790), Leonhard Euler (1707–1783), Mikhail Lomonosov (1711–1765) and Jean le Rond d'Alembert (1717–1783), epitomized in the appearance of Denis Diderot's Encyclopédie between 1751 and 1772.
label: sentence

sentence: The impact of this process was not limited to science and technology, but affected philosophy (Immanuel Kant, David Hume), religion (the increasingly significant impact of science upon religion), and society and politics in general (Adam Smith, Voltaire), the French Revolution of 1789 setting a bloody cesura indicating the beginning of political modernity[citation needed].
label: sentence

sentence: The early modern period is seen as a flowering of the European Renaissance, in what is often known as the Scientific Revolution, viewed as a foundation of modern science.
label: sentence

sentence: The Romantic Movement of the early 19th century reshaped science by opening up new pursuits unexpected in the classical approaches of the Enlightenment.
label: sentence

sentence: Major breakthroughs came in biology, especially in Darwin's theory of evolution, as well as physics (electromagnetism), mathematics (non-Euclidean geometry, group theory) and chemistry (organic chemistry).
label: sentence

sentence: The decline of Romanticism occurred because a new movement, Positivism, began to take hold of the ideals of the intellectuals after 1840 and lasted until about 1880.
label: sentence

sentence: The scientific revolution is a convenient boundary between ancient thought and classical physics.
label: sentence

sentence: Nicolaus Copernicus revived the heliocentric model of the solar system described by Aristarchus of Samos.
label: sentence

sentence: This was followed by the first known model of planetary motion given by Johannes Kepler in the early 17th century, which proposed that the planets follow elliptical orbits, with the Sun at one focus of the ellipse.
label: sentence

sentence: Galileo ("Father of Modern Physics") also made use of experiments to validate physical theories, a key element of the scientific method.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1687, Isaac Newton published the Principia Mathematica, detailing two comprehensive and successful physical theories: Newton's laws of motion, which led to classical mechanics; and Newton's Law of Gravitation, which describes the fundamental force of gravity.
label: sentence

sentence: The behavior of electricity and magnetism was studied by Faraday, Ohm, and others during the early 19th century.
label: sentence

sentence: These studies led to the unification of the two phenomena into a single theory of electromagnetism, by James Clerk Maxwell (known as Maxwell's equations).
label: sentence

sentence: The beginning of the 20th century brought the start of a revolution in physics.
label: sentence

sentence: The long-held theories of Newton were shown not to be correct in all circumstances.
label: sentence

sentence: Beginning in 1900, Max Planck, Albert Einstein, Niels Bohr and others developed quantum theories to explain various anomalous experimental results, by introducing discrete energy levels.
label: sentence

sentence: Not only did quantum mechanics show that the laws of motion did not hold on small scales, but even more disturbingly, the theory of general relativity, proposed by Einstein in 1915, showed that the fixed background of spacetime, on which both Newtonian mechanics and special relativity depended, could not exist.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1925, Werner Heisenberg and Erwin Schrödinger formulated quantum mechanics, which explained the preceding quantum theories.
label: sentence

sentence: The observation by Edwin Hubble in 1929 that the speed at which galaxies recede positively correlates with their distance, led to the understanding that the universe is expanding, and the formulation of the Big Bang theory by Georges Lemaître.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1938 Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann discovered nuclear fission with radiochemical methods, and in 1939 Lise Meitner and Otto Robert Frisch wrote the first theoretical interpretation of the fission process, which was later improved by Niels Bohr and John A. Wheeler.
label: sentence

sentence: Further developments took place during World War II, which led to the practical application of radar and the development and use of the atomic bomb.
label: sentence

sentence: Though the process had begun with the invention of the cyclotron by Ernest O. Lawrence in the 1930s, physics in the postwar period entered into a phase of what historians have called "Big Science", requiring massive machines, budgets, and laboratories in order to test their theories and move into new frontiers.
label: sentence

sentence: The primary patron of physics became state governments, who recognized that the support of "basic" research could often lead to technologies useful to both military and industrial applications.
label: sentence

sentence: Currently, general relativity and quantum mechanics are inconsistent with each other, and efforts are underway to unify the two.
label: sentence

sentence: Modern chemistry emerged from the sixteenth through the eighteenth centuries through the material practices and theories promoted by alchemy, medicine, manufacturing and mining.
label: sentence

sentence: A decisive moment came when 'chymistry' was distinguished from alchemy by Robert Boyle in his work The Sceptical Chymist, in 1661; although the alchemical tradition continued for some time after his work.
label: sentence

sentence: Other important steps included the gravimetric experimental practices of medical chemists like William Cullen, Joseph Black, Torbern Bergman and Pierre Macquer and through the work of Antoine Lavoisier (Father of Modern Chemistry) on oxygen and the law of conservation of mass, which refuted phlogiston theory.
label: sentence

sentence: The theory that all matter is made of atoms, which are the smallest constituents of matter that cannot be broken down without losing the basic chemical and physical properties of that matter, was provided by John Dalton in 1803, although the question took a hundred years to settle as proven.
label: sentence

sentence: Dalton also formulated the law of mass relationships.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1869, Dmitri Mendeleev composed his periodic table of elements on the basis of Dalton's discoveries.
label: sentence

sentence: The synthesis of urea by Friedrich Wöhler opened a new research field, organic chemistry, and by the end of the 19th century, scientists were able to synthesize hundreds of organic compounds.
label: sentence

sentence: The later part of the 19th century saw the exploitation of the Earth's petrochemicals, after the exhaustion of the oil supply from whaling.
label: sentence

sentence: By the 20th century, systematic production of refined materials provided a ready supply of products which provided not only energy, but also synthetic materials for clothing, medicine, and everyday disposable resources.
label: sentence

sentence: Application of the techniques of organic chemistry to living organisms resulted in physiological chemistry, the precursor to biochemistry.
label: sentence

sentence: The 20th century also saw the integration of physics and chemistry, with chemical properties explained as the result of the electronic structure of the atom.
label: sentence

sentence: Linus Pauling's book on The Nature of the Chemical Bond used the principles of quantum mechanics to deduce bond angles in ever-more complicated molecules.
label: sentence

sentence: Pauling's work culminated in the physical modelling of DNA, the secret of life (in the words of Francis Crick, 1953).
label: sentence

sentence: In the same year, the Miller–Urey experiment demonstrated in a simulation of primordial processes, that basic constituents of proteins, simple amino acids, could themselves be built up from simpler molecules.
label: sentence

sentence: Geology existed as a cloud of isolated, disconnected ideas about rocks, minerals, and landforms long before it became a coherent science.
label: sentence

sentence: Theophrastus' work on rocks, Peri lithōn, remained authoritative for millennia: its interpretation of fossils was not overturned until after the Scientific Revolution.
label: sentence

sentence: Chinese polymath Shen Kua (1031–1095) first formulated hypotheses for the process of land formation.
label: sentence

sentence: Based on his observation of fossils in a geological stratum in a mountain hundreds of miles from the ocean, he deduced that the land was formed by erosion of the mountains and by deposition of silt.
label: sentence

sentence: Geology did not undergo systematic restructuring during the Scientific Revolution, but individual theorists made important contributions.
label: sentence

sentence: Robert Hooke, for example, formulated a theory of earthquakes, and Nicholas Steno developed the theory of superposition and argued that fossils were the remains of once-living creatures.
label: sentence

sentence: Beginning with Thomas Burnet's Sacred Theory of the Earth in 1681, natural philosophers began to explore the idea that the Earth had changed over time.
label: sentence

sentence: Burnet and his contemporaries interpreted Earth's past in terms of events described in the Bible, but their work laid the intellectual foundations for secular interpretations of Earth history.
label: sentence

sentence: Modern geology, like modern chemistry, gradually evolved during the 18th and early 19th centuries.
label: sentence

sentence: Benoît de Maillet and the Comte de Buffon saw the Earth as much older than the 6,000 years envisioned by biblical scholars.
label: sentence

sentence: Jean-Étienne Guettard and Nicolas Desmarest hiked central France and recorded their observations on some of the first geological maps.
label: sentence

sentence: Aided by chemical experimentation, naturalists such as Scotland's John Walker, Sweden's Torbern Bergman, and Germany's Abraham Werner created comprehensive classification systems for rocks and minerals—a collective achievement that transformed geology into a cutting edge field by the end of the eighteenth century.
label: sentence

sentence: These early geologists also proposed a generalized interpretations of Earth history that led James Hutton, Georges Cuvier and Alexandre Brongniart, following in the steps of Steno, to argue that layers of rock could be dated by the fossils they contained: a principle first applied to the geology of the Paris Basin.
label: sentence

sentence: The use of index fossils became a powerful tool for making geological maps, because it allowed geologists to correlate the rocks in one locality with those of similar age in other, distant localities.
label: sentence

sentence: Over the first half of the 19th century, geologists such as Charles Lyell, Adam Sedgwick, and Roderick Murchison applied the new technique to rocks throughout Europe and eastern North America, setting the stage for more detailed, government-funded mapping projects in later decades.
label: sentence

sentence: Midway through the 19th century, the focus of geology shifted from description and classification to attempts to understand how the surface of the Earth had changed.
label: sentence

sentence: The first comprehensive theories of mountain building were proposed during this period, as were the first modern theories of earthquakes and volcanoes.
label: sentence

sentence: Louis Agassiz and others established the reality of continent-covering ice ages, and "fluvialists" like Andrew Crombie Ramsay argued that river valleys were formed, over millions of years by the rivers that flow through them.
label: sentence

sentence: After the discovery of radioactivity, radiometric dating methods were developed, starting in the 20th century.
label: sentence

sentence: Alfred Wegener's theory of "continental drift" was widely dismissed when he proposed it in the 1910s, but new data gathered in the 1950s and 1960s led to the theory of plate tectonics, which provided a plausible mechanism for it.
label: sentence

sentence: Plate tectonics also provided a unified explanation for a wide range of seemingly unrelated geological phenomena.
label: sentence

sentence: Since 1970 it has served as the unifying principle in geology.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1847, Hungarian physician Ignác Fülöp Semmelweis dramatically reduced the occurrency of puerperal fever by simply requiring physicians to wash their hands before attending to women in childbirth.
label: sentence

sentence: This discovery predated the germ theory of disease.
label: sentence

sentence: However, Semmelweis' findings were not appreciated by his contemporaries and came into use only with discoveries by British surgeon Joseph Lister, who in 1865 proved the principles of antisepsis.
label: sentence

sentence: Lister's work was based on the important findings by French biologist Louis Pasteur.
label: sentence

sentence: Pasteur was able to link microorganisms with disease, revolutionizing medicine.
label: sentence

sentence: He also devised one of the most important methods in preventive medicine, when in 1880 he produced a vaccine against rabies.
label: sentence

sentence: Pasteur invented the process of pasteurization, to help prevent the spread of disease through milk and other foods.
label: sentence

sentence: Perhaps the most prominent, controversial and far-reaching theory in all of science has been the theory of evolution by natural selection put forward by the British naturalist Charles Darwin in his book On the Origin of Species in 1859.
label: sentence

sentence: Darwin proposed that the features of all living things, including humans, were shaped by natural processes over long periods of time.
label: sentence

sentence: The theory of evolution in its current form affects almost all areas of biology.
label: sentence

sentence: Implications of evolution on fields outside of pure science have led to both opposition and support from different parts of society, and profoundly influenced the popular understanding of "man's place in the universe".
label: sentence

sentence: In the early 20th century, the study of heredity became a major investigation after the rediscovery in 1900 of the laws of inheritance developed by the Moravian monk Gregor Mendel in 1866.
label: sentence

sentence: Mendel's laws provided the beginnings of the study of genetics, which became a major field of research for both scientific and industrial research.
label: sentence

sentence: By 1953, James D. Watson, Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins clarified the basic structure of DNA, the genetic material for expressing life in all its forms.
label: sentence

sentence: In the late 20th century, the possibilities of genetic engineering became practical for the first time, and a massive international effort began in 1990 to map out an entire human genome (the Human Genome Project).
label: sentence

sentence: The discipline of ecology typically traces its origin to the synthesis of Darwinian evolution and Humboldtian biogeography, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
label: sentence

sentence: Equally important in the rise of ecology, however, were microbiology and soil science—particularly the cycle of life concept, prominent in the work Louis Pasteur and Ferdinand Cohn.
label: sentence

sentence: The word ecology was coined by Ernst Haeckel, whose particularly holistic view of nature in general (and Darwin's theory in particular) was important in the spread of ecological thinking.
label: sentence

sentence: In the 1930s, Arthur Tansley and others began developing the field of ecosystem ecology, which combined experimental soil science with physiological concepts of energy and the techniques of field biology.
label: sentence

sentence: The history of ecology in the 20th century is closely tied to that of environmentalism; the Gaia hypothesis, first formulated in the 1960s, and spreading in the 1970s, and more recently the scientific-religious movement of Deep Ecology have brought the two closer together.
label: sentence

sentence: Political science is a late arrival in terms of social sciences[citation needed].
label: sentence

sentence: However, the discipline has a clear set of antecedents such as moral philosophy, political philosophy, political economy, history, and other fields concerned with normative determinations of what ought to be and with deducing the characteristics and functions of the ideal form of government.
label: sentence

sentence: The roots of politics are in prehistory.
label: sentence

sentence: In each historic period and in almost every geographic area, we can find someone studying politics and increasing political understanding.
label: sentence

sentence: In Western culture, the study of politics is first found in Ancient Greece.
label: sentence

sentence: The antecedents of European politics trace their roots back even earlier than Plato and Aristotle, particularly in the works of Homer, Hesiod, Thucydides, Xenophon, and Euripides.
label: sentence

sentence: Later, Plato analyzed political systems, abstracted their analysis from more literary- and history- oriented studies and applied an approach we would understand as closer to philosophy.
label: sentence

sentence: Similarly, Aristotle built upon Plato's analysis to include historical empirical evidence in his analysis.
label: sentence

sentence: An ancient Indian treatise on statecraft, economic policy and military strategy by Kautilya and Viṣhṇugupta, who are traditionally identified with Chāṇakya (c. 350–-283 BCE).
label: sentence

sentence: In this treatise, the behaviors and relationships of the people, the King, the State, the Government Superintendents, Courtiers, Enemies, Invaders, and Corporations are analysed and documented.
label: sentence

sentence: Roger Boesche describes the Arthaśāstra as "a book of political realism, a book analysing how the political world does work and not very often stating how it ought to work, a book that frequently discloses to a king what calculating and sometimes brutal measures he must carry out to preserve the state and the common good."
label: sentence

sentence: With the fall of the Western Roman Empire, there arose a more diffuse arena for political studies.
label: sentence

sentence: The rise of monotheism and, particularly for the Western tradition, Christianity, brought to light a new space for politics and political action[citation needed].
label: sentence

sentence: During the Middle Ages, the study of politics was widespread in the churches and courts.
label: sentence

sentence: Works such as Augustine of Hippo's The City of God synthesized current philosophies and political traditions with those of Christianity, redefining the borders between what was religious and what was political.
label: sentence

sentence: Most of the political questions surrounding the relationship between Church and State were clarified and contested in this period.
label: sentence

sentence: Historical linguistics emerged as an independent field of study at the end of the 18th century.
label: sentence

sentence: Sir William Jones proposed that Sanskrit, Persian, Greek, Latin, Gothic, and Celtic languages all shared a common base.
label: sentence

sentence: After Jones, an effort to catalog all languages of the world was made throughout the 19th century and into the 20th century.
label: sentence

sentence: Publication of Ferdinand de Saussure's Cours de linguistique générale created the development of descriptive linguistics.
label: sentence

sentence: Descriptive linguistics, and the related structuralism movement caused linguistics to focus on how language changes over time, instead of just describing the differences between languages.
label: sentence

sentence: Noam Chomsky further diversified linguistics with the development of generative linguistics in the 1950s.
label: sentence

sentence: His effort is based upon a mathematical model of language that allows for the description and prediction of valid syntax.
label: sentence

sentence: Additional specialties such as sociolinguistics, cognitive linguistics, and computational linguistics have emerged from collaboration between linguistics and other disciplines.
label: sentence

sentence: The basis for classical economics forms Adam Smith's An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, published in 1776.
label: sentence

sentence: Smith criticized mercantilism, advocating a system of free trade with division of labour.
label: sentence

sentence: He postulated an "invisible hand" that regulated economic systems made up of actors guided only by self-interest.
label: sentence

sentence: Textual criticism is a branch of textual scholarship, philology, and literary criticism that is concerned with the identification of textual variants in either manuscripts or printed books.
label: sentence

sentence: Ancient scribes made alterations when copying manuscripts by hand.
label: sentence

sentence: Given a manuscript copy, several or many copies, but not the original document, the textual critic might seek to reconstruct the original text (the archetype or autograph) as closely as possible.
label: sentence

sentence: The same processes can be used to attempt to reconstruct intermediate versions, or recensions, of a document's transcription history.
label: sentence

sentence: The ultimate objective of the textual critic's work is the production of a "critical edition" containing a scholarly curated text.
label: sentence

sentence: Many ancient works, such as the Bible and the Greek tragedies,[citation needed] survive in hundreds of copies, and the relationship of each copy to the original may be unclear.
label: sentence

sentence: Textual scholars have debated for centuries which sources are most closely derived from the original, hence which readings in those sources are correct.
label: sentence

sentence: [citation needed] Although biblical books that are letters, like Greek plays, presumably had one original, the question of whether some biblical books, like the Gospels, ever had just one original has been discussed.
label: sentence

sentence: Interest in applying textual criticism to the Qur'an has also developed after the discovery of the Sana'a manuscripts in 1972, which possibly date back to the 7–8th centuries.
label: sentence

sentence: In the English language, the works of Shakespeare have been a particularly fertile ground for textual criticism—both because the texts, as transmitted, contain a considerable amount of variation, and because the effort and expense of producing superior editions of his works have always been widely viewed as worthwhile.
label: sentence

sentence: The principles of textual criticism, although originally developed and refined for works of antiquity, the Bible, and Shakespeare, have been applied to many works, extending backwards from the present to the earliest known written documents, in Mesopotamia and Egypt—a period of about five millennia.
label: sentence

sentence: However, the application of textual criticism to non-religious works does not antedate the invention of printing.
label: sentence

sentence: While Christianity has been relatively receptive to textual criticism, application of it to the Jewish (Masoretic) Torah and the Qur'an is, to the devout, taboo.
label: sentence

sentence: [citation needed]

sentence: Maas comments further that "A dictation revised by the author must be regarded as equivalent to an autograph manuscript".

sentence: The lack of autograph manuscripts applies to many cultures other than Greek and Roman.

sentence: In such a situation, a key objective becomes the identification of the first exemplar before any split in the tradition.
label: sentence

sentence: That exemplar is known as the archetype.
label: sentence

sentence: "If we succeed in establishing the text of [the archetype], the constitutio (reconstruction of the original) is considerably advanced.

sentence: The textual critic's ultimate objective is the production of a "critical edition".
label: sentence

sentence: [citation needed] This contains the text that the author has determined most closely approximates the original, and is accompanied by an apparatus criticus or critical apparatus.
label: sentence

sentence: The critical apparatus presents the author's work in three parts: first, a list or description of the evidence that the editor used (names of manuscripts, or abbreviations called sigla); second, the editor's analysis of that evidence (sometimes a simple likelihood rating),[citation needed]; and third, a record of rejected variants of the text (often in order of preference).

sentence: [citation needed]

sentence: Before mechanical printing, literature was copied by hand, and many variations were introduced by copyists.
label: sentence

sentence: The age of printing made the scribal profession effectively redundant.
label: sentence

sentence: Printed editions, while less susceptible to the proliferation of variations likely to arise during manual transmission, are nonetheless not immune to introducing variations from an author's autograph.
label: sentence

sentence: Instead of a scribe miscopying his source, a compositor or a printing shop may read or typeset a work in a way that differs from the autograph.
label: sentence

sentence: Since each scribe or printer commits different errors, reconstruction of the lost original is often aided by a selection of readings taken from many sources.
label: sentence

sentence: An edited text that draws from multiple sources is said to be eclectic.
label: sentence

sentence: In contrast to this approach, some textual critics prefer to identify the single best surviving text, and not to combine readings from multiple sources.
label: sentence

sentence: When comparing different documents, or "witnesses", of a single, original text, the observed differences are called variant readings, or simply variants or readings.
label: sentence

sentence: It is not always apparent which single variant represents the author's original work.
label: sentence

sentence: The process of textual criticism seeks to explain how each variant may have entered the text, either by accident (duplication or omission) or intention (harmonization or censorship), as scribes or supervisors transmitted the original author's text by copying it.
label: sentence

sentence: The textual critic's task, therefore, is to sort through the variants, eliminating those most likely to be un-original, hence establishing a "critical text", or critical edition, that is intended to best approximate the original.
label: sentence

sentence: At the same time, the critical text should document variant readings, so the relation of extant witnesses to the reconstructed original is apparent to a reader of the critical edition.
label: sentence

sentence: In establishing the critical text, the textual critic considers both "external" evidence (the age, provenance, and affiliation of each witness) and "internal" or "physical" considerations (what the author and scribes, or printers, were likely to have done).
label: sentence

sentence: The collation of all known variants of a text is referred to as a variorum, namely a work of textual criticism whereby all variations and emendations are set side by side so that a reader can track how textual decisions have been made in the preparation of a text for publication.
label: sentence

sentence: The Bible and the works of William Shakespeare have often been the subjects of variorum editions, although the same techniques have been applied with less frequency to many other works, such as Walt Whitman's Leaves of Grass, and the prose writings of Edward Fitzgerald.
label: sentence

sentence: Eclectic readings also normally give an impression of the number of witnesses to each available reading.
label: sentence

sentence: Although a reading supported by the majority of witnesses is frequently preferred, this does not follow automatically.
label: sentence

sentence: For example, a second edition of a Shakespeare play may include an addition alluding to an event known to have happened between the two editions.
label: sentence

sentence: Although nearly all subsequent manuscripts may have included the addition, textual critics may reconstruct the original without the addition.
label: sentence

sentence: External evidence is evidence of each physical witness, its date, source, and relationship to other known witnesses.
label: sentence

sentence: Critics will often prefer the readings supported by the oldest witnesses.
label: sentence

sentence: Since errors tend to accumulate, older manuscripts should have fewer errors.
label: sentence

sentence: Readings supported by a majority of witnesses are also usually preferred, since these are less likely to reflect accidents or individual biases.
label: sentence

sentence: For the same reasons, the most geographically diverse witnesses are preferred.
label: sentence

sentence: Some manuscripts show evidence that particular care was taken in their composition, for example, by including alternative readings in their margins, demonstrating that more than one prior copy (exemplar) was consulted in producing the current one.
label: sentence

sentence: Other factors being equal, these are the best witnesses.
label: sentence

sentence: The role of the textual critic is necessary when these basic criteria are in conflict.

sentence: For instance, there will typically be fewer early copies, and a larger number of later copies.
label: sentence

sentence: The textual critic will attempt to balance these criteria, to determine the original text.

sentence: Two common considerations have the Latin names lectio brevior (shorter reading) and lectio difficilior (more difficult reading).

sentence: The first is the general observation that scribes tended to add words, for clarification or out of habit, more often than they removed them.

sentence: The second, lectio difficilior potior (the harder reading is stronger), recognizes the tendency for harmonization—resolving apparent inconsistencies in the text.
label: sentence

sentence: Applying this principle leads to taking the more difficult (unharmonized) reading as being more likely to be the original.

sentence: Such cases also include scribes simplifying and smoothing texts they did not fully understand.

sentence: Stemmatics, stemmology or stemmatology is a rigorous approach to textual criticism.
label: sentence

sentence: Karl Lachmann (1793–1851) greatly contributed to making this method famous, even though he did not invent it.
label: sentence

sentence: The method takes its name from the word stemma.
label: sentence

sentence: The Ancient Greek word στέμματα and its loanword in classical Latin stemmata may refer to "family trees".
label: sentence

sentence: This specific meaning shows the relationships of the surviving witnesses (the first known example of such a stemma, albeit with the name, dates from 1827).
label: sentence

sentence: The family tree is also referred to as a cladogram.
label: sentence

sentence: The method works from the principle that "community of error implies community of origin."
label: sentence

sentence: That is, if two witnesses have a number of errors in common, it may be presumed that they were derived from a common intermediate source, called a hyparchetype.
label: sentence

sentence: Relations between the lost intermediates are determined by the same process, placing all extant manuscripts in a family tree or stemma codicum descended from a single archetype.
label: sentence

sentence: The process of constructing the stemma is called recension, or the Latin recensio.
label: sentence

sentence: The process of selectio resembles eclectic textual criticism, but applied to a restricted set of hypothetical hyparchetypes.
label: sentence

sentence: The steps of examinatio and emendatio resemble copy-text editing.

sentence: In fact, the other techniques can be seen as special cases of stemmatics in which a rigorous family history of the text cannot be determined but only approximated.
label: sentence

sentence: If it seems that one manuscript is by far the best text, then copy text editing is appropriate, and if it seems that a group of manuscripts are good, then eclecticism on that group would be proper.

sentence: The critic Joseph Bédier (1864–1938) launched a particularly withering attack on stemmatics in 1928.
label: sentence

sentence: He surveyed editions of medieval French texts that were produced with the stemmatic method, and found that textual critics tended overwhelmingly to produce trees divided into just two branches.
label: sentence

sentence: He concluded that this outcome was unlikely to have occurred by chance, and that therefore, the method was tending to produce bipartite stemmas regardless of the actual history of the witnesses.
label: sentence

sentence: He suspected that editors tended to favor trees with two branches, as this would maximize the opportunities for editorial judgment (as there would be no third branch to "break the tie" whenever the witnesses disagreed).
label: sentence

sentence: He also noted that, for many works, more than one reasonable stemma could be postulated, suggesting that the method was not as rigorous or as scientific as its proponents had claimed.
label: sentence

sentence: The stemmatic method's final step is emendatio, also sometimes referred to as "conjectural emendation."
label: sentence

sentence: But in fact, the critic employs conjecture at every step of the process.
label: sentence

sentence: Some of the method's rules that are designed to reduce the exercise of editorial judgment do not necessarily produce the correct result.

sentence: For example, where there are more than two witnesses at the same level of the tree, normally the critic will select the dominant reading.

sentence: However, it may be no more than fortuitous that more witnesses have survived that present a particular reading.

sentence: A plausible reading that occurs less often may, nevertheless, be the correct one.

sentence: The bibliographer Ronald B. McKerrow introduced the term copy-text in his 1904 edition of the works of Thomas Nashe, defining it as "the text used in each particular case as the basis of mine."

sentence: McKerrow was aware of the limitations of the stemmatic method, and believed it was more prudent to choose one particular text that was thought to be particularly reliable, and then to emend it only where the text was obviously corrupt.

sentence: Hindu philosophy refers to a group of darśanas (philosophies, world views, teachings) that emerged in ancient India.
label: sentence

sentence: The mainstream Hindu philosophy includes six systems (ṣaḍdarśana) – Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa and Vedanta.
label: sentence

sentence: These are also called the Astika (orthodox) philosophical traditions and are those that accept the Vedas as authoritative, important source of knowledge.
label: sentence

sentence: [note 1][note 2] Ancient and medieval India was also the source of philosophies that share philosophical concepts but rejected the Vedas, and these have been called nāstika (heterodox or non-orthodox) Indian philosophies.
label: sentence

sentence: Nāstika Indian philosophies include Buddhism, Jainism, Cārvāka, Ājīvika, and others.
label: sentence

sentence: Scholars have debated the relationship and differences within āstika philosophies and with nāstika philosophies, starting with the writings of Indologists and Orientalists of the 18th and 19th centuries, which were themselves derived from limited availability of Indian literature and medieval doxographies.
label: sentence

sentence: The various sibling traditions included in Hindu philosophies are diverse, and they are united by shared history and concepts, same textual resources, similar ontological and soteriological focus, and cosmology.
label: sentence

sentence: While Buddhism and Jainism are considered distinct philosophies and religions, some heterodox traditions such as Cārvāka are often considered as distinct schools within Hindu philosophy.
label: sentence

sentence: Hindu philosophy also includes several sub-schools of theistic philosophies that integrate ideas from two or more of the six orthodox philosophies, such as the realism of the Nyāya, the naturalism of the Vaiśeṣika, the dualism of the Sāṅkhya, the monism and knowledge of Self as essential to liberation of Advaita, the self-discipline of yoga and the asceticism and elements of theistic ideas.
label: sentence

sentence: Examples of such schools include Pāśupata Śaiva, Śaiva siddhānta, Pratyabhijña, Raseśvara and Vaiṣṇava.
label: sentence

sentence: Some sub-schools share Tantric ideas with those found in some Buddhist traditions.
label: sentence

sentence: The ideas of these sub-schools are found in the Puranas and Āgamas.
label: sentence

sentence: Ancient and medieval Hindu texts identify six pramāṇas as correct means of accurate knowledge and truths: pratyakṣa (perception), anumāṇa (inference), upamāṇa (comparison and analogy), arthāpatti (postulation, derivation from circumstances), anupalabdi (non-perception, negative/cognitive proof) and śabda (word, testimony of past or present reliable experts) Each of these are further categorized in terms of conditionality, completeness, confidence and possibility of error, by each school .
label: sentence

sentence: The various schools vary on how many of these six are valid paths of knowledge.
label: sentence

sentence: For example, the Cārvāka nāstika philosophy holds that only one (perception) is an epistemically reliable means of knowledge, the Samkhya school holds three are (perception, inference and testimony), while the Mīmāṃsā and Advaita schools hold all six are epistemically useful and reliable means to knowledge.
label: sentence

sentence: Samkhya school espouses dualism between consciousness and matter.
label: sentence

sentence: It regards the universe as consisting of two realities; Puruṣa (consciousness) and prakriti (matter).
label: sentence

sentence: Jiva (a living being) is that state in which puruṣa is bonded to prakriti in some form.
label: sentence

sentence: This fusion, state the Samkhya scholars, led to the emergence of buddhi (awareness, intellect) and ahankara (individualized ego consciousness, “I-maker”).
label: sentence

sentence: The universe is described by this school as one created by Purusa-Prakriti entities infused with various permutations and combinations of variously enumerated elements, senses, feelings, activity and mind.
label: sentence

sentence: Samkhya philosophy includes a theory of gunas (qualities, innate tendencies, psyche).
label: sentence

sentence: Guna, it states, are of three types: Sattva being good, compassionate, illuminating, positive, and constructive; Rajas guna is one of activity, chaotic, passion, impulsive, potentially good or bad; and Tamas being the quality of darkness, ignorance, destructive, lethargic, negative.
label: sentence

sentence: Everything, all life forms and human beings, state Samkhya scholars, have these three gunas, but in different proportions.
label: sentence

sentence: The interplay of these gunas defines the character of someone or something, of nature and determines the progress of life.
label: sentence

sentence: Samkhya theorises a pluralism of souls (Jeevatmas) who possess consciousness, but denies the existence of Ishvara (God).
label: sentence

sentence: Classical Samkhya is considered an atheist / non-theistic Hindu philosophy.
label: sentence

sentence: In Indian philosophy, Yoga is among other things, the name of one of the six āstika philosophical schools.
label: sentence

sentence: The Yoga philosophical system is closely allied with the dualism premises of Samkhya school.
label: sentence

sentence: The Yoga school accepts the Samkhya psychology and metaphysics, but is considered theistic because it accepts the concept of "personal god", unlike Samkhya.
label: sentence

sentence: The epistemology of the Yoga school, like the Sāmkhya school, relies on three of six prāmaṇas as the means of gaining reliable knowledge: pratyakṣa (perception), anumāṇa (inference) and śabda (āptavacana, word/testimony of reliable sources).
label: sentence

sentence: The Yoga school builds on the Samkhya school theory that jñāna (knowledge) is a sufficient means to moksha.
label: sentence

sentence: It suggests that systematic techniques/practice (personal experimentation) combined with Samkhya's approach to knowledge is the path to moksha.
label: sentence

sentence: Yoga shares several central ideas with Advaita Vedanta, with the difference that Yoga is a form of experimental mysticism while Advaita Vedanta is a form of monistic personalism.
label: sentence

sentence: Like Advaita Vedanta, the Yoga school of Hindu philosophy states that liberation/freedom in this life is achievable, and this occurs when an individual fully understands and realizes the equivalence of Atman (soul, self) and Brahman.
label: sentence

sentence: The Vaiśeṣika philosophy is a naturalist school; it is a form of atomism in natural philosophy.
label: sentence

sentence: It postulated that all objects in the physical universe are reducible to paramāṇu (atoms), and one's experiences are derived from the interplay of substance (a function of atoms, their number and their spatial arrangements), quality, activity, commonness, particularity and inherence.
label: sentence

sentence: Knowledge and liberation was achievable by complete understanding of the world of experience, according to Vaiśeṣika school .
label: sentence

sentence: The Vaiśeṣika darśana is credited to Kaṇāda Kaśyapa from the second half of the first millennium BCE.
label: sentence

sentence: The foundational text, the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, opens as follows,
label: sentence

sentence: Vaiśeṣika metaphysical premises are founded on a form of atomism, that the reality is composed of four substances (earth, water, air, fire).
label: sentence

sentence: Each of these four are of two types: atomic (paramāṇu) and composite.

sentence: An atom is, according to Vaiśeṣika scholars, that which is indestructible (anitya), indivisible, and has a special kind of dimension, called “small” (aṇu).
label: sentence

sentence: A composite, in this philosophy, is defined to be anything which is divisible into atoms.

sentence: Whatever human beings perceive is composite, while atoms are invisible.

sentence: The Vaiśeṣikas stated that size, form, truths and everything that human beings experience as a whole is a function of atoms, their number and their spatial arrangements, their guṇa (quality), karma (activity), sāmānya (commonness), viśeṣa (particularity) and amavāya (inherence, inseparable connectedness of everything).

sentence: In its metaphysics, Nyāya school is closer to the Vaiśeṣika school than others.

sentence: It holds that human suffering results from mistakes/defects produced by activity under wrong knowledge (notions and ignorance).

sentence: Moksha (liberation), it states, is gained through right knowledge.

sentence: This premise led Nyāya to concern itself with epistemology, that is the reliable means to gain correct knowledge and to remove wrong notions.
label: sentence

sentence: False knowledge is not merely ignorance to Naiyayikas, it includes delusion.

sentence: Correct knowledge is discovering and overcoming one's delusions, and understanding true nature of soul, self and reality.

sentence: The Mīmāṃsā school has several subschools defined by epistemology.
label: sentence

sentence: The Prābhākara subschool of Mīmāṃsā considered five epistemically reliable means to gaining knowledge: pratyakṣa (perception), anumāṇa (inference), upamāṇa (comparison and analogy), arthāpatti (postulation, derivation from circumstances), and śabda (word, testimony of past or present reliable experts).
label: sentence

sentence: The Kumārila Bhaṭṭa sub-school of Mīmāṃsā added sixth to its canon of reliable epistemology - anupalabdi (non-perception, negative/cognitive proof).
label: sentence

sentence: The metaphysics in Mīmāṃsā school consists of both atheistic and theistic doctrines and the school showed little interest in systematic examination of the existence of God.

sentence: Rather, it held that the soul is eternal omnipresent, inherently active spiritual essence, then focussed on the epistemology and metaphysics of dharma.

sentence: To them, dharma meant rituals and duties, not devas (gods), because devas existed only in name.
label: sentence

sentence: They considered the Upanishads and other self-knowledge, spirituality-related texts to be of secondary importance, a philosophical view that the Vedanta school disagreed with.

sentence: Mīmāṃsā gave rise to the study of philology and the philosophy of language.

sentence: While their deep analysis of language and linguistics influenced other schools, their views were not shared by others.

sentence: Mīmāṃsākas considered the purpose and power of language was to clearly prescribe the proper, correct and right.

sentence: In contrast, Vedantins extended the scope and value of language as a tool to also describe, develop and derive.
label: sentence

sentence: Mīmāṃsākas considered orderly, law-driven, procedural life as central purpose and noblest necessity of dharma and society, and divine (theistic) sustenance means to that end.
label: sentence

sentence: The Mimamsa school was influential and foundational to the Vedanta school, with the difference that Mīmāṃsā school developed and emphasized karmakāṇḍa (that part of the śruti which relates to ceremonial acts and sacrificial rites, the early parts of the Vedas), while the Vedanta school developed and emphasized jñānakāṇḍa (that portion of the Vedas which relates to knowledge of monism, the latter parts of the Vedas).
label: sentence

sentence: The Vedānta school built upon the teachings of the Upanishads and Brahma Sutras from the first millennium BCE and is the most developed and well-known of the Hindu schools.
label: sentence

sentence: The epistemology of the Vedantins included, depending on the sub-school, five or six methods as proper and reliable means of gaining any form of knowledge: pratyakṣa (perception), anumāṇa (inference), upamāṇa (comparison and analogy), arthāpatti (postulation, derivation from circumstances), anupalabdi (non-perception, negative/cognitive proof) and śabda (word, testimony of past or present reliable experts).

sentence: Each of these have been further categorized in terms of conditionality, completeness, confidence and possibility of error, by each sub-school of Vedanta.

sentence: Advaita literally means "not two, sole, unity".

sentence: It is a sub-school of Vedanta, and asserts spiritual and universal non-dualism.

sentence: He wrote extensive commentaries on the major Vedantic scriptures and is celebrated as one of the major Hindu philosophers from whose doctrines the main currents of modern Indian thought are derived.

sentence: The concept of ātman is of soul, self within each person, each living being.

sentence: Ramanuja (c. 1037–1137) was the foremost proponent of the philosophy of Viśiṣṭādvaita or qualified non-dualism.

sentence: They saw Brahman as an eternal oneness, but also as the source of all creation, which was omnipresent and actively involved in existence.

sentence: To them the sense of subject-object perception was illusory and a sign of ignorance.

sentence: However, the individual's sense of self was not a complete illusion since it was derived from the universal beingness that is Brahman.

sentence: Ramanuja saw Vishnu as a personification of Brahman.

sentence: Dvaita Vedanta is a dualistic interpretation of the Vedas, espouses dualism by theorizing the existence of two separate realities.

sentence: The first and the only independent reality, states the Dvaita school, is that of Vishnu or Brahman.

sentence: Vishnu is the supreme Self, in a manner similar to monotheistic God in other major religions.

sentence: The distinguishing factor of Dvaita philosophy, as opposed to monistic Advaita Vedanta, is that God takes on a personal role and is seen as a real eternal entity that governs and controls the universe.

sentence: Like Vishishtadvaita Vedanta subschool, Dvaita philosophy also embraced Vaishnavism, with the metaphysical concept of Brahman in the Vedas identified with Vishnu and the one and only Supreme Being.

sentence: According to this philosophy there are three categories of existence: Brahman, soul, and matter.

sentence: The philosophy of Pashupata sect was systematized by Lakulish in the 2nd century CE.

sentence: Paśu in Paśupati refers to the effect (or created world), the word designates that which is dependent on something ulterior.

sentence: The first political factions, cohering around a basic, if fluid, set of principles emerged from the Exclusion Crisis and Glorious Revolution in late-17th-century England.

sentence: The Whigs supported Protestant constitutional monarchy against absolute rule and the Tories, originating in the Royalist (or "Cavalier") faction of the English Civil War, were conservative royalist supporters of a strong monarchy as a counterbalance to the republican tendencies of Whigs, who were the dominant political faction for most of the first half of the 18th century; they supported the Hanoverian succession of 1715 against the Jacobite supporters of the deposed Roman Catholic Stuart dynasty and were able to purge Tory politicians from important government positions after the failed Jacobite rising of 1715.

sentence: Galicia (English i/ɡəˈlɪsiə/, /ɡəˈlɪʃə/; Galician: [ɡaˈliθja] ( listen), [ħaˈliθja], or [ħaˈlisja]; Spanish: [ɡaˈliθja]; Galician and Portuguese: Galiza, [ɡaˈliθa] ( listen), [ħaˈliθa] or [ħaˈlisa]) is an autonomous community of Spain and historic nationality under Spanish law.
label: sentence

sentence: Located in the North-West of the Iberian Peninsula, it comprises the provinces of A Coruña, Lugo, Ourense and Pontevedra, being bordered by Portugal to the south, the Spanish autonomous communities of Castile and León and Asturias to the east, and the Atlantic Ocean to the west and the north.
label: sentence

sentence: It had a population of 2,765,940 in 2013 and has a total area of 29,574 km2 (11,419 sq mi).
label: sentence

sentence: Galicia has over 1,660 km (1,030 mi) of coastline, including its offshore islands and islets, among them Cíes Islands, Ons, Sálvora, Cortegada, and—the largest and most populated—A Illa de Arousa.
label: sentence

sentence: The area now called Galicia was first inhabited by humans during the Middle Paleolithic period, and it takes its name from the Gallaeci, the Celtic peoples living north of the Douro river during the last millennium BC, in a region largely coincidental with that of the Iron Age local Castro culture.
label: sentence

sentence: Galicia was incorporated into the Roman Empire at the end of the Cantabrian Wars in 19 BC, being turned into a Roman province in the 3rd century AD.
label: sentence

sentence: In 410, the Germanic Suebi established a kingdom with its capital in Braga (Portugal) which was incorporated into that of the Visigoths in 585.
label: sentence

sentence: In 711, the Arabs invaded the Iberian Peninsula, taking the Visigoth kingdom, but soon in 740 Galicia was incorporated into the Christian kingdom of Asturias.
label: sentence

sentence: During the Middle Ages, the kingdom of Galicia was occasionally ruled by its own kings, but most of the time it was leagued to the kingdom of Leon and later to that of Castile, while maintaining its own legal and customary practices and personality.
label: sentence

sentence: From the 13th century on, the kings of Castile, as kings of Galicia, appointed an Adiantado-mór, whose attributions passed to the Governor and Captain General of the Kingdom of Galiza from the last years of the 15th century.
label: sentence

sentence: The Governor also presided the Real Audiencia do Reino de Galicia, a royal tribunal and government body.
label: sentence

sentence: From the 16th century, the representation and voice of the kingdom was held by an assembly of deputies and representatives of the cities of the kingdom, the Cortes or Junta of the Kingdom of Galicia, an institution which was forcibly discontinued in 1833 when the kingdom was divided into four administrative provinces with no legal mutual links.
label: sentence

sentence: During the 19th and 20th centuries, demand grew for self-government and for the recognition of the personality of Galicia, a demand which led to the frustrated Statute of Autonomy of 1936, and to the Statute of Autonomy of 1981, currently in force.

sentence: The interior of Galicia is characterized by its hilly landscape, although mountain ranges rise to 2,000 m (6,600 ft) in the east and south.
label: sentence

sentence: The coastal areas are mostly an alternate series of rías (submerged valleys where the sea penetrates tens of kilometres inland) and cliffs.
label: sentence

sentence: The climate of Galicia is temperate and rainy, but it is also markedly drier in the summer, being usually classified as Oceanic in the west and north, and Mediterranean in the southeast.
label: sentence

sentence: Its topographic and climatic conditions have made animal husbandry and farming the primary source of Galicia's wealth for most of its history.
label: sentence

sentence: With the exception of shipbuilding and food processing, Galicia was largely a semi-subsistence farming and fishing economy and did not experience significant industrialization until after the mid-20th century.
label: sentence

sentence: In 2012, the gross domestic product at purchasing power parity was €56,000 million, with a nominal GDP per capita of €20,700.

sentence: The population is largely concentrated in two coastal areas: from Ferrol to A Coruña in the northwest and from Pontevedra to Vigo in the southwest.

sentence: To a lesser extent, there are smaller populations around the interior cities of Lugo, Ourense and Santiago de Compostela.

sentence: The name evolved during the Middle Ages from Gallaecia, sometimes written Galletia, to Gallicia.

sentence: On the other hand, the lack of an effective royal justice system in the Kingdom led to the social conflict known as the Guerras Irmandiñas ('Wars of the brotherhoods'), when leagues of peasants and burghers, with the support of a number of knights, noblemen, and under legal protection offered by the remote king, toppled many of the castles of the Kingdom and briefly drove the noblemen into Portugal and Castile.

sentence: From that moment Galicia, which participated to a minor extent in the American expansion of the Spanish Empire, found itself at the center of the Atlantic wars fought by Spain against the French and the Protestant powers of England and the Netherlands, whose privateers attacked the coastal areas, but major assaults were not common as the coastline was difficult and the harbors easily defended.

sentence: USB was designed to standardize the connection of computer peripherals (including keyboards, pointing devices, digital cameras, printers, portable media players, disk drives and network adapters) to personal computers, both to communicate and to supply electric power.

sentence: Unicode is a computing industry standard for the consistent encoding, representation, and handling of text expressed in most of the world's writing systems.
label: sentence

sentence: Developed in conjunction with the Universal Coded Character Set (UCS) standard and published as The Unicode Standard, the latest version of Unicode contains a repertoire of more than 120,000 characters covering 129 modern and historic scripts, as well as multiple symbol sets.
label: sentence

sentence: The standard consists of a set of code charts for visual reference, an encoding method and set of standard character encodings, a set of reference data files, and a number of related items, such as character properties, rules for normalization, decomposition, collation, rendering, and bidirectional display order (for the correct display of text containing both right-to-left scripts, such as Arabic and Hebrew, and left-to-right scripts).
label: sentence

sentence: As of June 2015[update], the most recent version is Unicode 8.0.
label: sentence

sentence: The standard is maintained by the Unicode Consortium.
label: sentence

sentence: Unicode can be implemented by different character encodings.
label: sentence

sentence: The most commonly used encodings are UTF-8, UTF-16 and the now-obsolete UCS-2.
label: sentence

sentence: UTF-8 uses one byte for any ASCII character, all of which have the same code values in both UTF-8 and ASCII encoding, and up to four bytes for other characters.
label: sentence

sentence: UCS-2 uses a 16-bit code unit (two 8-bit bytes) for each character but cannot encode every character in the current Unicode standard.
label: sentence

sentence: UTF-16 extends UCS-2, using one 16-bit unit for the characters that were representable in UCS-2 and two 16-bit units (4 × 8 bits) to handle each of the additional characters.
label: sentence

sentence: Unicode has the explicit aim of transcending the limitations of traditional character encodings, such as those defined by the ISO 8859 standard, which find wide usage in various countries of the world but remain largely incompatible with each other.
label: sentence

sentence: Many traditional character encodings share a common problem in that they allow bilingual computer processing (usually using Latin characters and the local script), but not multilingual computer processing (computer processing of arbitrary scripts mixed with each other).
label: sentence

sentence: The first 256 code points were made identical to the content of ISO-8859-1 so as to make it trivial to convert existing western text.
label: sentence

sentence: Many essentially identical characters were encoded multiple times at different code points to preserve distinctions used by legacy encodings and therefore, allow conversion from those encodings to Unicode (and back) without losing any information.
label: sentence

sentence: For example, the "fullwidth forms" section of code points encompasses a full Latin alphabet that is separate from the main Latin alphabet section because in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean (CJK) fonts, these Latin characters are rendered at the same width as CJK ideographs, rather than at half the width.
label: sentence

sentence: For other examples, see Duplicate characters in Unicode.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1996, a surrogate character mechanism was implemented in Unicode 2.0, so that Unicode was no longer restricted to 16 bits.
label: sentence

sentence: This increased the Unicode codespace to over a million code points, which allowed for the encoding of many historic scripts (e.g., Egyptian Hieroglyphs) and thousands of rarely used or obsolete characters that had not been anticipated as needing encoding.
label: sentence

sentence: Among the characters not originally intended for Unicode are rarely used Kanji or Chinese characters, many of which are part of personal and place names, making them rarely used, but much more essential than envisioned in the original architecture of Unicode.
label: sentence

sentence: Each code point has a single General Category property.
label: sentence

sentence: The major categories are: Letter, Mark, Number, Punctuation, Symbol, Separator and Other.
label: sentence

sentence: Within these categories, there are subdivisions.

sentence: The General Category is not useful for every use, since legacy encodings have used multiple characteristics per single code point.
label: sentence

sentence: E.g., U+000A <control-000A> Line feed (LF) in ASCII is both a control and a formatting separator; in Unicode the General Category is "Other, Control".
label: sentence

sentence: Often, other properties must be used to specify the characteristics and behaviour of a code point.

sentence: The possible General Categories are:
