sentence: Albert Einstein proposed that the laws of physics should be based on the principle of relativity.
label: sentence

sentence: This principle holds that the rules of physics must be the same for all observers, regardless of the frame of reference that is used, and that light propagates at the same speed in all reference frames.
label: sentence

sentence: This theory was motivated by Maxwell's equations, which show that electromagnetic waves propagate in a vacuum at the speed of light.
label: sentence

sentence: However, Maxwell's equations give no indication of what this speed is relative to.
label: sentence

sentence: Prior to Einstein, it was thought that this speed was relative to a fixed medium, called the luminiferous ether.
label: sentence

sentence: In contrast, the theory of special relativity postulates that light propagates at the speed of light in all inertial frames, and examines the implications of this postulate.
label: sentence

sentence: In classical physics, an inertial reference frame is one in which an object that experiences no forces does not accelerate.
label: sentence

sentence: In general relativity, an inertial frame of reference is one that is following a geodesic of space-time.
label: sentence

sentence: An object that moves against a geodesic experiences a force.
label: sentence

sentence: An object in free fall does not experience a force, because it is following a geodesic.
label: sentence

sentence: An object standing on the earth, however, will experience a force, as it is being held against the geodesic by the surface of the planet.
label: sentence

sentence: In light of this, the bucket of water rotating in empty space will experience a force because it rotates with respect to the geodesic.
label: sentence

sentence: The water will become concave, not because it is rotating with respect to the distant stars, but because it is rotating with respect to the geodesic.
label: sentence

sentence: Einstein partially advocates Mach's principle in that distant stars explain inertia because they provide the gravitational field against which acceleration and inertia occur.

sentence: The problem of the direction of time arises directly from two contradictory facts.
label: sentence

sentence: Firstly, the fundamental physical laws are time-reversal invariant; if a cinematographic film were taken of any process describable by means of the aforementioned laws and then played backwards, it would still portray a physically possible process.
label: sentence

sentence: Secondly, our experience of time, at the macroscopic level, is not time-reversal invariant.
label: sentence

sentence: Glasses can fall and break, but shards of glass cannot reassemble and fly up onto tables.
label: sentence

sentence: We have memories of the past, and none of the future.
label: sentence

sentence: We feel we can't change the past but can influence the future.

sentence: But in statistical mechanics things get more complicated.
label: sentence

sentence: On one hand, statistical mechanics is far superior to classical thermodynamics, in that thermodynamic behavior, such as glass breaking, can be explained by the fundamental laws of physics paired with a statistical postulate.
label: sentence

sentence: But statistical mechanics, unlike classical thermodynamics, is time-reversal symmetric.
label: sentence

sentence: The second law of thermodynamics, as it arises in statistical mechanics, merely states that it is overwhelmingly likely that net entropy will increase, but it is not an absolute law.

sentence: A third type of solution to the problem of the direction of time, although much less represented, argues that the laws are not time-reversal symmetric.

sentence: For example, certain processes in quantum mechanics, relating to the weak nuclear force, are not time-reversible, keeping in mind that when dealing with quantum mechanics time-reversibility comprises a more complex definition.

sentence: But this type of solution is insufficient because 1) the time-asymmetric phenomena in quantum mechanics are too few to account for the uniformity of macroscopic time-asymmetry and 2) it relies on the assumption that quantum mechanics is the final or correct description of physical processes.

sentence: The problem of the flow of time, as it has been treated in analytic philosophy, owes its beginning to a paper written by J. M. E. McTaggart.

sentence: In this paper McTaggart proposes two "temporal series".

sentence: The first series, which means to account for our intuitions about temporal becoming, or the moving Now, is called the A-series.

sentence: According to Presentism, time is an ordering of various realities.

sentence: The positions on the persistence of objects are somewhat similar.

sentence: An endurantist holds that for an object to persist through time is for it to exist completely at different times (each instance of existence we can regard as somehow separate from previous and future instances, though still numerically identical with them).

sentence: A perdurantist on the other hand holds that for a thing to exist through time is for it to exist as a continuous reality, and that when we consider the thing as a whole we must consider an aggregate of all its "temporal parts" or instances of existing.

sentence: However, asymmetry of causation can be observed in a non-arbitrary way which is not metaphysical in the case of a human hand dropping a cup of water which smashes into fragments on a hard floor, spilling the liquid.

sentence: Traditionally considered the last part of the Stone Age, the Neolithic followed the terminal Holocene Epipaleolithic period and commenced with the beginning of farming, which produced the "Neolithic Revolution".

sentence: Philosophical empiricists hold no knowledge to be properly inferred or deduced unless it is derived from one's sense-based experience.

sentence: British empiricism, though it was not a term used at the time, derives from the 17th century period of early modern philosophy and modern science.

sentence: The term became useful in order to describe differences perceived between two of its founders Francis Bacon, described as empiricist, and René Descartes, who is described as a rationalist.

label: sentence

sentence: In response to the early-to-mid-17th century "continental rationalism" John Locke (1632–1704) proposed in An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689) a very influential view wherein the only knowledge humans can have is a posteriori, i.e., based upon experience.
label: sentence

sentence: Locke is famously attributed with holding the proposition that the human mind is a tabula rasa, a "blank tablet", in Locke's words "white paper", on which the experiences derived from sense impressions as a person's life proceeds are written.
label: sentence

sentence: There are two sources of our ideas: sensation and reflection.
label: sentence

sentence: In both cases, a distinction is made between simple and complex ideas.
label: sentence

sentence: The former are unanalysable, and are broken down into primary and secondary qualities.
label: sentence

sentence: Primary qualities are essential for the object in question to be what it is.
label: sentence

sentence: Without specific primary qualities, an object would not be what it is.
label: sentence

sentence: For example, an apple is an apple because of the arrangement of its atomic structure.
label: sentence

sentence: If an apple was structured differently, it would cease to be an apple.
label: sentence

sentence: Secondary qualities are the sensory information we can perceive from its primary qualities.
label: sentence

sentence: For example, an apple can be perceived in various colours, sizes, and textures but it is still identified as an apple.
label: sentence

sentence: Therefore, its primary qualities dictate what the object essentially is, while its secondary qualities define its attributes.
label: sentence

sentence: Complex ideas combine simple ones, and divide into substances, modes, and relations.
label: sentence

sentence: According to Locke, our knowledge of things is a perception of ideas that are in accordance or discordance with each other, which is very different from the quest for certainty of Descartes.
label: sentence

sentence: A generation later, the Irish Anglican bishop, George Berkeley (1685–1753), determined that Locke's view immediately opened a door that would lead to eventual atheism.
label: sentence

sentence: In response to Locke, he put forth in his Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710) an important challenge to empiricism in which things only exist either as a result of their being perceived, or by virtue of the fact that they are an entity doing the perceiving.

sentence: (For Berkeley, God fills in for humans by doing the perceiving whenever humans are not around to do it.)

sentence: Berkeley's approach to empiricism would later come to be called subjective idealism.

sentence: The Scottish philosopher David Hume (1711–1776) responded to Berkeley's criticisms of Locke, as well as other differences between early modern philosophers, and moved empiricism to a new level of skepticism.

sentence: And,
label: sentence

sentence: Mathematical and logical propositions (e.g.
label: sentence

label: sentence

sentence: Ideas are therefore the faint copies of sensations.

sentence: Hume maintained that all knowledge, even the most basic beliefs about the natural world, cannot be conclusively established by reason.

sentence: Rather, he maintained, our beliefs are more a result of accumulated habits, developed in response to accumulated sense experiences.
label: sentence

sentence: Among his many arguments Hume also added another important slant to the debate about scientific method — that of the problem of induction.
label: sentence

sentence: Hume argued that it requires inductive reasoning to arrive at the premises for the principle of inductive reasoning, and therefore the justification for inductive reasoning is a circular argument.
label: sentence

sentence: Among Hume's conclusions regarding the problem of induction is that there is no certainty that the future will resemble the past.

sentence: Thus, as a simple instance posed by Hume, we cannot know with certainty by inductive reasoning that the sun will continue to rise in the East, but instead come to expect it to do so because it has repeatedly done so in the past.

sentence: According to an extreme empiricist theory known as phenomenalism, anticipated by the arguments of both Hume and George Berkeley, a physical object is a kind of construction out of our experiences.
label: sentence

sentence: Phenomenalism is the view that physical objects, properties, events (whatever is physical) are reducible to mental objects, properties, events.
label: sentence

label: sentence

sentence: By the phenomenalistic line of thinking, to have a visual experience of a real physical thing is to have an experience of a certain kind of group of experiences.
label: sentence

sentence: This type of set of experiences possesses a constancy and coherence that is lacking in the set of experiences of which hallucinations, for example, are a part.

sentence: As John Stuart Mill put it in the mid-19th century, matter is the "permanent possibility of sensation".

sentence: As summarized by D.W. Hamlin:
label: sentence

sentence: Mill's empiricism thus held that knowledge of any kind is not from direct experience but an inductive inference from direct experience.

sentence: The problems other philosophers have had with Mill's position center around the following issues: Firstly, Mill's formulation encounters difficulty when it describes what direct experience is by differentiating only between actual and possible sensations.

sentence: Berkeley put God in that gap; the phenomenalists, including Mill, essentially left the question unanswered.

sentence: Offering financial incentives, he successfully convinced 8 African states to break off diplomatic relations with Israel in 1973.
label: sentence

sentence: Intent on propagating Islam, in 1973 Gaddafi founded the Islamic Call Society, which had opened 132 centres across Africa within a decade.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1973 he converted Gabonese President Omar Bongo, an action which he repeated three years later with Jean-Bédel Bokassa, president of the Central African Republic.
label: sentence

sentence: Gaddafi sought to develop closer links in the Maghreb; in January 1974 Libya and Tunisia announced a political union, the Arab Islamic Republic.
label: sentence

sentence: Although advocated by Gaddafi and Tunisian President Habib Bourguiba, the move was deeply unpopular in Tunisia and soon abandoned.
label: sentence

sentence: Retaliating, Gaddafi sponsored anti-government militants in Tunisia into the 1980s.
label: sentence

sentence: Turning his attention to Algeria, in 1975 Libya signed the Hassi Messaoud defence agreement allegedly to counter "Moroccan expansionism", also funding the Polisario Front of Western Sahara in their independence struggle against Morocco.
label: sentence

sentence: Seeking to diversify Libya's economy, Gaddafi's government began purchasing shares in major European corporations like Fiat as well as buying real estate in Malta and Italy, which would become a valuable source of income during the 1980s oil slump.
label: sentence

sentence: On 2 March 1977 the General People's Congress adopted the "Declaration of the Establishment of the People's Authority" at Gaddafi's behest.
label: sentence

sentence: Dissolving the Libyan Arab Republic, it was replaced by the Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya (Arabic: الجماهيرية العربية الليبية الشعبية الاشتراكية‎, al-Jamāhīrīyah al-‘Arabīyah al-Lībīyah ash-Sha‘bīyah al-Ishtirākīyah), a "state of the masses" conceptualized by Gaddafi.
label: sentence

sentence: Officially, the Jamahiriya was a direct democracy in which the people ruled themselves through the 187 Basic People's Congresses, where all adult Libyans participated and voted on national decisions.
label: sentence

sentence: These then sent members to the annual General People's Congress, which was broadcast live on television.
label: sentence

sentence: In principle, the People's Congresses were Libya's highest authority, with major decisions proposed by government officials or with Gaddafi himself requiring the consent of the People's Congresses.
label: sentence

sentence: Debate remained limited, and major decisions regarding the economy and defence were avoided or dealt with cursorily; the GPC largely remained "a rubber stamp" for Gaddafi's policies.
label: sentence

sentence: On rare occasions, the GPC opposed Gaddafi's suggestions, sometimes successfully; notably, when Gaddafi called on primary schools to be abolished, believing that home schooling was healthier for children, the GPC rejected the idea.
label: sentence

sentence: In other instances, Gaddafi pushed through laws without the GPC's support, such as when he desired to allow women into the armed forces.
label: sentence

sentence: Gaddafi proclaimed that the People's Congresses provided for Libya's every political need, rendering other political organizations unnecessary; all non-authorized groups, including political parties, professional associations, independent trade unions and women's groups, were banned.
label: sentence

sentence: With preceding legal institutions abolished, Gaddafi envisioned the Jamahiriya as following the Qur'an for legal guidance, adopting sharia law; he proclaimed "man-made" laws unnatural and dictatorial, only permitting Allah's law.
label: sentence

sentence: Within a year he was backtracking, announcing that sharia was inappropriate for the Jamahiriya because it guaranteed the protection of private property, contravening The Green Book's socialism.
label: sentence

sentence: His emphasis on placing his own work on a par with the Qur'an led conservative clerics to accuse him of shirk, furthering their opposition to his regime.
label: sentence

sentence: In July, a border war broke out with Egypt, in which the Egyptians defeated Libya despite their technological inferiority.
label: sentence

sentence: The conflict lasted one week before both sides agreed to sign a peace treaty that was brokered by several Arab states.
label: sentence

sentence: That year, Gaddafi was invited to Moscow by the Soviet government in recognition of their increasing commercial relationship.
label: sentence

sentence: In December 1978, Gaddafi stepped down as Secretary-General of the GPC, announcing his new focus on revolutionary rather than governmental activities; this was part of his new emphasis on separating the apparatus of the revolution from the government.
label: sentence

sentence: Although no longer in a formal governmental post, he adopted the title of "Leader of the Revolution" and continued as commander-in-chief of the armed forces.
label: sentence

sentence: He continued exerting considerable influence over Libya, with many critics insisting that the structure of Libya's direct democracy gave him "the freedom to manipulate outcomes".
label: sentence

sentence: Libya began to turn towards socialism.
label: sentence

sentence: In March 1978, the government issued guidelines for housing redistribution, attempting to ensure the population that every adult Libyan owned his own home and that nobody was enslaved to paying their rent.
label: sentence

sentence: Most families were banned from owning more than one house, while former rental properties were seized and sold to the tenants at a heavily subsidized price.
label: sentence

sentence: In September, Gaddafi called for the People's Committees to eliminate the "bureaucracy of the public sector" and the "dictatorship of the private sector"; the People's Committees took control of several hundred companies, converting them into worker cooperatives run by elected representatives.
label: sentence

sentence: On 2 March 1979, the GPC announced the separation of government and revolution, the latter being represented by new Revolutionary Committees, who operated in tandem with the People's Committees in schools, universities, unions, the police force and the military.
label: sentence

sentence: Dominated by revolutionary zealots, the Revolutionary Committees were led by Mohammad Maghgoub and a Central Coordinating Office, and met with Gaddafi annually.
label: sentence

sentence: Publishing a weekly magazine The Green March (al-Zahf al-Akhdar), in October 1980 they took control of the press.
label: sentence

sentence: Responsible for perpetuating revolutionary fervour, they performed ideological surveillance, later adopting a significant security role, making arrests and putting people on trial according to the "law of the revolution" (qanun al-thawra).
label: sentence

sentence: With no legal code or safeguards, the administration of revolutionary justice was largely arbitrary and resulted in widespread abuses and the suppression of civil liberties: the "Green Terror."
label: sentence

sentence: In 1979, the committees began the redistribution of land in the Jefara plain, continuing through 1981.
label: sentence

sentence: In May 1980, measures to redistribute and equalize wealth were implemented; anyone with over 1000 dinar in his bank account saw that extra money expropriated.
label: sentence

sentence: The following year, the GPC announced that the government would take control of all import, export and distribution functions, with state supermarkets replacing privately owned businesses; this led to a decline in the availability of consumer goods and the development of a thriving black market.
label: sentence

sentence: The Jamahiriya's radical direction earned the government many enemies.
label: sentence

sentence: In February 1978, Gaddafi discovered that his head of military intelligence was plotting to kill him, and began to increasingly entrust security to his Qaddadfa tribe.
label: sentence

sentence: Many who had seen their wealth and property confiscated turned against the administration, and a number of western-funded opposition groups were founded by exiles.
label: sentence

sentence: Most prominent was the National Front for the Salvation of Libya (NFSL), founded in 1981 by Mohammed Magariaf, which orchestrated militant attacks against Libya's government, while another, al-Borkan, began killing Libyan diplomats abroad.
label: sentence

sentence: Following Gaddafi's command to kill these "stray dogs", under Colonel Younis Bilgasim's leadership, the Revolutionary Committees set up overseas branches to suppress counter-revolutionary activity, assassinating various dissidents.
label: sentence

sentence: Although nearby nations like Syria also used hit squads, Gaddafi was unusual in publicly bragging about his administration's use of them; in June 1980, he ordered all dissidents to return home or be "liquidated wherever you are."
label: sentence

sentence: In 1979, the U.S. placed Libya on its list of "State Sponsors of Terrorism", while at the end of the year a demonstration torched the U.S. embassy in Tripoli in solidarity with the perpetrators of the Iran hostage crisis.
label: sentence

sentence: The following year, Libyan fighters began intercepting U.S. fighter jets flying over the Mediterranean, signalling the collapse of relations between the two countries.
label: sentence

sentence: Libyan relations with Lebanon and Shi'ite communities across the world also deteriorated due to the August 1978 disappearance of imam Musa al-Sadr when visiting Libya; the Lebanese accused Gaddafi of having him killed or imprisoned, a charge he denied.
label: sentence

sentence: Relations with Syria improved, as Gaddafi and Syrian President Hafez al-Assad shared an enmity with Israel and Egypt's Sadat.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1980, they proposed a political union, with Libya paying off Syria's £1 billion debt to the Soviet Union; although pressures led Assad to pull out, they remained allies.
label: sentence

sentence: Another key ally was Uganda, and in 1979, Gaddafi sent 2,500 troops into Uganda to defend the regime of President Idi Amin from Tanzanian invaders.
label: sentence

sentence: The mission failed; 400 Libyans were killed and they were forced to retreat.
label: sentence

sentence: Gaddafi later came to regret his alliance with Amin, openly criticising him.
label: sentence

sentence: The early and mid-1980s saw economic trouble for Libya; from 1982 to 1986, the country's annual oil revenues dropped from $21 billion to $5.4 billion.
label: sentence

sentence: Focusing on irrigation projects, 1983 saw construction start on "Gaddafi's Pet Project", the Great Man-Made River; although designed to be finished by the end of the decade, it remained incomplete at the start of the 21st century.
label: sentence

sentence: Military spending increased, while other administrative budgets were cut back.
label: sentence

sentence: Libya had long supported the FROLINAT militia in neighbouring Chad, and in December 1980, re-invaded Chad at the request of the Frolinat-controlled GUNT government to aid in the civil war; in January 1981, Gaddafi suggested a political merger.
label: sentence

sentence: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) rejected this, and called for a Libyan withdrawal, which came about in November 1981.
label: sentence

sentence: The civil war resumed, and so Libya sent troops back in, clashing with French forces who supported the southern Chadian forces.
label: sentence

sentence: Many African nations had tired of Libya's policies of interference in foreign affairs; by 1980, nine African states had cut off diplomatic relations with Libya, while in 1982 the OAU cancelled its scheduled conference in Tripoli in order to prevent Gaddafi gaining chairmanship.
label: sentence

sentence: Proposing political unity with Morocco, in August 1984, Gaddafi and Moroccan monarch Hassan II signed the Oujda Treaty, forming the Arab-African Union; such a union was considered surprising due to the strong political differences and longstanding enmity that existed between the two governments.
label: sentence

sentence: Relations remained strained, particularly due to Morocco's friendly relations with the U.S. and Israel; in August 1986, Hassan abolished the union.
label: sentence

sentence: Domestic threats continued to plague Gaddafi; in May 1984, his Bab al-Azizia home was unsuccessfully attacked by a joint NFSL–Muslim Brotherhood militia, and in the aftermath 5000 dissidents were arrested.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1981, the new US President Ronald Reagan pursued a hard line approach to Libya, erroneously considering it a puppet regime of the Soviet Union.
label: sentence

sentence: In turn, Gaddafi played up his commercial relationship with the Soviets, visiting Moscow again in April 1981 and 1985, and threatening to join the Warsaw Pact.
label: sentence

sentence: The Soviets were nevertheless cautious of Gaddafi, seeing him as an unpredictable extremist.
label: sentence

sentence: Beginning military exercises in the Gulf of Sirte – an area of sea that Libya claimed as a part of its territorial waters – in August 1981 the U.S. shot down two Libyan Su-22 planes monitoring them.
label: sentence

sentence: Closing down Libya's embassy in Washington, D.C., Reagan advised U.S. companies operating in the country to reduce the number of American personnel stationed there.
label: sentence

sentence: In March 1982, the U.S. implemented an embargo of Libyan oil, and in January 1986 ordered all U.S. companies to cease operating in the country, although several hundred workers remained.
label: sentence

sentence: Diplomatic relations also broke down with the U.K., after Libyan diplomats were accused in the shooting death of Yvonne Fletcher, a British policewoman stationed outside their London embassy, in April 1984.
label: sentence

sentence: In Spring 1986, the U.S. Navy again began performing exercises in the Gulf of Sirte; the Libyan military retaliated, but failed as the U.S. sank several Libyan ships.
label: sentence

sentence: After the U.S. accused Libya of orchestrating the 1986 Berlin discotheque bombing, in which two American soldiers died, Reagan decided to retaliate militarily.
label: sentence

sentence: The Central Intelligence Agency were critical of the move, believing that Syria were a greater threat and that an attack would strengthen Gaddafi's reputation; however Libya was recognised as a "soft target."
label: sentence

sentence: Reagan was supported by the U.K. but opposed by other European allies, who argued that it would contravene international law.
label: sentence

sentence: In Operation El Dorado Canyon, orchestrated on 15 April 1986, U.S. military planes launched a series of air-strikes on Libya, bombing military installations in various parts of the country, killing around 100 Libyans, including several civilians.
label: sentence

sentence: One of the targets had been Gaddafi's home.
label: sentence

sentence: Himself unharmed, two of Gaddafi's sons were injured, and he claimed that his four-year-old adopted daughter Hanna was killed, although her existence has since been questioned.
label: sentence

sentence: In the immediate aftermath, Gaddafi retreated to the desert to meditate, while there were sporadic clashes between Gaddafists and army officers who wanted to overthrow the government.
label: sentence

sentence: Although the U.S. was condemned internationally, Reagan received a popularity boost at home.
label: sentence

sentence: Publicly lambasting U.S. imperialism, Gaddafi's reputation as an anti-imperialist was strengthened both domestically and across the Arab world, and in June 1986, he ordered the names of the month to be changed in Libya.
label: sentence

sentence: The late 1980s saw a series of liberalising economic reforms within Libya designed to cope with the decline in oil revenues.
label: sentence

sentence: In May 1987, Gaddafi announced the start of the "Revolution within a Revolution", which began with reforms to industry and agriculture and saw the re-opening of small business.
label: sentence

sentence: Restrictions were placed on the activities of the Revolutionary Committees; in March 1988, their role was narrowed by the newly created Ministry for Mass Mobilization and Revolutionary Leadership to restrict their violence and judicial role, while in August 1988 Gaddafi publicly criticised them, asserting that "they deviated, harmed, tortured" and that "the true revolutionary does not practise repression."
label: sentence

sentence: In March, hundreds of political prisoners were freed, with Gaddafi falsely claiming that there were no further political prisoners in Libya.
label: sentence

sentence: In June, Libya's government issued the Great Green Charter on Human Rights in the Era of the Masses, in which 27 articles laid out goals, rights and guarantees to improve the situation of human rights in Libya, restricting the use of the death penalty and calling for its eventual abolition.
label: sentence

sentence: Many of the measures suggested in the charter would be implemented the following year, although others remained inactive.
label: sentence

sentence: Also in 1989, the government founded the Al-Gaddafi International Prize for Human Rights, to be awarded to figures from the Third World who had struggled against colonialism and imperialism; the first year's winner was South African anti-apartheid activist Nelson Mandela.
label: sentence

sentence: From 1994 through to 1997, the government initiated cleansing committees to root out corruption, particularly in the economic sector.
label: sentence

sentence: In the aftermath of the 1986 U.S. attack, the army was purged of perceived disloyal elements, and in 1988, Gaddafi announced the creation of a popular militia to replace the army and police.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1987, Libya began production of mustard gas at a facility in Rabta, although publicly denying it was stockpiling chemical weapons, and unsuccessfully attempted to develop nuclear weapons.
label: sentence

sentence: The period also saw a growth in domestic Islamist opposition, formulated into groups like the Muslim Brotherhood and the Libyan Islamic Fighting Group.
label: sentence

sentence: A number of assassination attempts against Gaddafi were foiled, and in turn, 1989 saw the security forces raid mosques believed to be centres of counter-revolutionary preaching.
label: sentence

sentence: In October 1993, elements of the increasingly marginalised army initiated a failed coup in Misrata, while in September 1995, Islamists launched an insurgency in Benghazi, and in July 1996 an anti-Gaddafist football riot broke out in Tripoli.
label: sentence

sentence: The Revolutionary Committees experienced a resurgence to combat these Islamists.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1989, Gaddafi was overjoyed by the foundation of the Arab Maghreb Union, uniting Libya in an economic pact with Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia and Algeria, viewing it as beginnings of a new Pan-Arab union.
label: sentence

sentence: Meanwhile, Libya stepped up its support for anti-western militants such as the Provisional IRA, and in 1988, Pan Am Flight 103 was blown up over Lockerbie in Scotland, killing 243 passengers and 16 crew members, plus 11 people on the ground.
label: sentence

sentence: British police investigations identified two Libyans – Abdelbaset al-Megrahi and Lamin Khalifah Fhimah – as the chief suspects, and in November 1991 issued a declaration demanding that Libya hand them over.
label: sentence

sentence: When Gaddafi refused, citing the Montreal Convention, the United Nations (UN) imposed Resolution 748 in March 1992, initiating economic sanctions against Libya which had deep repercussions for the country's economy.
label: sentence

sentence: The country suffered an estimated $900 million financial loss as a result.
label: sentence

sentence: Further problems arose with the west when in January 1989, two Libyan warplanes were shot down by the U.S. off the Libyan coast.
label: sentence

sentence: Many African states opposed the UN sanctions, with Mandela criticising them on a visit to Gaddafi in October 1997, when he praised Libya for its work in fighting apartheid and awarded Gaddafi the Order of Good Hope.
label: sentence

sentence: They would only be suspended in 1998 when Libya agreed to allow the extradition of the suspects to the Scottish Court in the Netherlands, in a process overseen by Mandela.
label: sentence

sentence: As the 20th century came to a close, Gaddafi increasingly rejected Arab nationalism, frustrated by the failure of his Pan-Arab ideals; instead he turned to Pan-Africanism, emphasising Libya's African identity.
label: sentence

sentence: From 1997 to 2000, Libya initiated cooperative agreements or bilateral aid arrangements with 10 African states, and in 1999 joined the Community of Sahel-Saharan States.
label: sentence

sentence: In June 1999, Gaddafi visited Mandela in South Africa, and the following month attended the OAU summit in Algiers, calling for greater political and economic integration across the continent and advocating the foundation of a United States of Africa.
label: sentence

sentence: He became one of the founders of the African Union (AU), initiated in July 2002 to replace the OAU; at the opening ceremonies, he proclaimed that African states should reject conditional aid from the developed world, a direct contrast to the message of South African President Thabo Mbeki.
label: sentence

sentence: At the third AU summit, held in Libya in July 2005, he called for a greater level of integration, advocating a single AU passport, a common defence system and a single currency, utilising the slogan: "The United States of Africa is the hope."
label: sentence

sentence: In June 2005, Libya joined the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA), and in August 2008 Gaddafi was proclaimed "King of Kings" by an assembled committee of traditional African leaders.
label: sentence

sentence: On 1 February 2009, his "coronation ceremony" was held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, coinciding with Gaddafi's election as AU chairman for a year.
label: sentence

sentence: The era saw Libya's return to the international arena.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1999, Libya began secret talks with the British government to normalise relations.
label: sentence

sentence: In 2001, Gaddafi condemned the September 11 attacks on the U.S. by al-Qaeda, expressing sympathy with the victims and calling for Libyan involvement in the War on Terror against militant Islamism.
label: sentence

sentence: His government continued suppressing domestic Islamism, at the same time as Gaddafi called for the wider application of sharia law.
label: sentence

sentence: Libya also cemented connections with China and North Korea, being visited by Chinese President Jiang Zemin in April 2002.
label: sentence

sentence: Influenced by the events of the Iraq War, in December 2003, Libya renounced its possession of weapons of mass destruction, decommissioning its chemical and nuclear weapons programs.
label: sentence

sentence: Relations with the U.S. improved as a result, while UK Prime Minister Tony Blair met with Gaddafi in the Libyan desert in March 2004.
label: sentence

sentence: The following month, Gaddafi travelled to the headquarters of the European Union (EU) in Brussels, signifying improved relations between Libya and the EU, the latter ending its remaining sanctions in October.
label: sentence

sentence: In October 2010, the EU paid Libya €50 million to stop African migrants passing into Europe; Gaddafi encouraged the move, saying that it was necessary to prevent the loss of European cultural identity to a new "Black Europe".
label: sentence

sentence: Removed from the U.S. list of state sponsors of terrorism in 2006, Gaddafi nevertheless continued his anti-western rhetoric, and at the Second Africa-South America Summit in Venezuela in September 2009, joined Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez in calling for an "anti-imperialist" front across Africa and Latin America.
label: sentence

sentence: Gaddafi proposed the establishment of a South Atlantic Treaty Organization to rival NATO.
label: sentence

sentence: That month he also addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York for the first time, using it to condemn "western aggression".
label: sentence

sentence: In Spring 2010, Gaddafi proclaimed jihad against Switzerland after Swiss police accused two of his family members of criminal activity in the country, resulting in the breakdown of bilateral relations.
label: sentence

sentence: Libya's economy witnessed increasing privatization; although rejecting the socialist policies of nationalized industry advocated in The Green Book, government figures asserted that they were forging "people's socialism" rather than capitalism.
label: sentence

sentence: Gaddafi welcomed these reforms, calling for wide-scale privatization in a March 2003 speech.
label: sentence

sentence: In 2003, the oil industry was largely sold to private corporations, and by 2004, there was $40 billion of direct foreign investment in Libya, a sixfold rise over 2003.
label: sentence

sentence: Sectors of Libya's population reacted against these reforms with public demonstrations, and in March 2006, revolutionary hard-liners took control of the GPC cabinet; although scaling back the pace of the changes, they did not halt them.
label: sentence

sentence: In 2010, plans were announced that would have seen half the Libyan economy privatized over the following decade.
label: sentence

sentence: While there was no accompanying political liberalization, with Gaddafi retaining predominant control, in March 2010, the government devolved further powers to the municipal councils.
label: sentence

sentence: Rising numbers of reformist technocrats attained positions in the country's governance; best known was Gaddafi's son and heir apparent Saif al-Islam Gaddafi, who was openly critical of Libya's human rights record.
label: sentence

sentence: He led a group who proposed the drafting of the new constitution, although it was never adopted, and in October 2009 was appointed to head the PSLC.
label: sentence

sentence: Involved in encouraging tourism, Saif founded several privately run media channels in 2008, but after criticising the government they were nationalised in 2009.
label: sentence

sentence: In October 2010, Gaddafi apologized to African leaders on behalf of Arab nations for their involvement in the African slave trade.
label: sentence

sentence: Following the start of the Arab Spring in 2011, Gaddafi spoke out in favour of Tunisian President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, then threatened by the Tunisian Revolution.
label: sentence

sentence: He suggested that Tunisia's people would be satisfied if Ben Ali introduced a Jamahiriyah system there.
label: sentence

sentence: Fearing domestic protest, Libya's government implemented preventative measures, reducing food prices, purging the army leadership of potential defectors and releasing several Islamist prisoners.
label: sentence

sentence: They proved ineffective, and on 17 February 2011, major protests broke out against Gaddafi's government.
label: sentence

sentence: Unlike Tunisia or Egypt, Libya was largely religiously homogenous and had no strong Islamist movement, but there was widespread dissatisfaction with the corruption and entrenched systems of patronage, while unemployment had reached around 30%.
label: sentence

sentence: Accusing the rebels of being "drugged" and linked to al-Qaeda, Gaddafi proclaimed that he would die a martyr rather than leave Libya.
label: sentence

sentence: As he announced that the rebels would be "hunted down street by street, house by house and wardrobe by wardrobe", the army opened fire on protests in Benghazi, killing hundreds.
label: sentence

sentence: Shocked at the government's response, a number of senior politicians resigned or defected to the protesters' side.
label: sentence

sentence: The uprising spread quickly through Libya's less economically developed eastern half.
label: sentence

sentence: By February's end, eastern cities like Benghazi, Misrata, al-Bayda and Tobruk were controlled by rebels, and the Benghazi-based National Transitional Council (NTC) had been founded to represent them.
label: sentence

sentence: In the conflict's early months it appeared that Gaddafi's government – with its greater firepower – would be victorious.
label: sentence

sentence: Both sides disregarded the laws of war, committing human rights abuses, including arbitrary arrests, torture, extrajudicial executions and revenge attacks.
label: sentence

sentence: On 26 February the United Nations Security Council passed Resolution 1970, suspending Libya from the UN Human Rights Council, implementing sanctions and calling for an International Criminal Court (ICC) investigation into the killing of unarmed civilians.
label: sentence

sentence: In March, the Security Council declared a no fly zone to protect the civilian population from aerial bombardment, calling on foreign nations to enforce it; it also specifically prohibited foreign occupation.
label: sentence

sentence: Ignoring this, Qatar sent hundreds of troops to support the dissidents, and along with France and the United Arab Emirates provided the NTC with weaponry and training.
label: sentence

sentence: A week after the implementation of the no-fly zone, NATO announced that it would be enforced.
label: sentence

sentence: On 30 April a NATO airstrike killed Gaddafi's sixth son and three of his grandsons in Tripoli, though Gaddafi and his wife were unharmed.
label: sentence

sentence: Western officials remained divided over whether Gaddafi was a legitimate military target under the U.N. Security Council resolution.
label: sentence

sentence: U.S. Secretary of Defense Robert Gates said that NATO was "not targeting Gaddafi specifically" but that his command-and-control facilities were legitimate targets—including a facility inside his sprawling Tripoli compound that was hit with airstrikes on 25 April.
label: sentence

sentence: On 27 June, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Gaddafi, his son Saif al-Islam, and his brother-in-law Abdullah Senussi, head of state security, for charges concerning crimes against humanity.
label: sentence

sentence: Libyan officials rejected the ICC, claiming that it had "no legitimacy whatsoever" and highlighting that "all of its activities are directed at African leaders".
label: sentence

sentence: That month, Amnesty International published their findings, in which they asserted that many of the accusations of mass human rights abuses made against Gaddafist forces lacked credible evidence, and were instead fabrications of the rebel forces which had been readily adopted by the western media.
label: sentence

sentence: Amnesty International did however still accuse Gaddafi forces of numerous war crimes.
label: sentence

sentence: On 15 July 2011, at a meeting in Istanbul, over 30 governments recognised the NTC as the legitimate government of Libya.
label: sentence

sentence: Gaddafi responded to the announcement with a speech on Libyan national television, in which he called on supporters to "Trample on those recognitions, trample on them under your feet ...
label: sentence

sentence: They are worthless".
label: sentence

sentence: Now with NATO support in the form of air cover, the rebel militia pushed westward, defeating loyalist armies and securing control of the centre of the country.
label: sentence

sentence: Gaining the support of Amazigh (Berber) communities of the Nafusa Mountains, who had long been persecuted as non-Arabic speakers under Gaddafi, the NTC armies surrounded Gaddafi loyalists in several key areas of western Libya.
label: sentence

sentence: In August, the rebels seized Zliten and Tripoli, ending the last vestiges of Gaddafist power.
label: sentence

sentence: On 25 August, the Arab League recognised the NTC to be "the legitimate representative of the Libyan state", on which basis Libya would resume its membership in the League.
label: sentence

sentence: Only a few towns in western Libya—such as Bani Walid, Sebha and Sirte—remained Gaddafist strongholds.
label: sentence

sentence: Retreating to Sirte after Tripoli's fall, Gaddafi announced his willingness to negotiate for a handover to a transitional government, a suggestion rejected by the NTC.
label: sentence

sentence: Surrounding himself with bodyguards, he continually moved residences to escape NTC shelling, devoting his days to prayer and reading the Qur'an.
label: sentence

sentence: On 20 October, Gaddafi broke out of Sirte's District 2 in a joint civilian-military convoy, hoping to take refuge in the Jarref Valley.
label: sentence

sentence: At around 8.30am, NATO bombers attacked, destroying at least 14 vehicles and killing at least 53.
label: sentence

sentence: The convoy scattered, and Gaddafi and those closest to him fled to a nearby villa, which was shelled by rebel militia from Misrata.
label: sentence

sentence: Fleeing to a construction site, Gaddafi and his inner cohort hid inside drainage pipes while his bodyguards battled the rebels; in the conflict, Gaddafi suffered head injuries from a grenade blast while defence minister Abu-Bakr Yunis Jabr was killed.
label: sentence

sentence: A Misratan militia took Gaddafi prisoner, beating him, causing serious injuries; the events were filmed on a mobile phone.
label: sentence

sentence: A video appears to picture Gaddafi being poked or stabbed in the rear end "with some kind of stick or knife" or possibly a bayonet.
label: sentence

sentence: Pulled onto the front of a pick-up truck, he fell off as it drove away.
label: sentence

sentence: His semi-naked, lifeless body was then placed into an ambulance and taken to Misrata; upon arrival, he was found to be dead.
label: sentence

sentence: Official NTC accounts claimed that Gaddafi was caught in a cross-fire and died from his bullet wounds.
label: sentence

sentence: Other eye-witness accounts claimed that rebels had fatally shot Gaddafi in the stomach; a rebel identifying himself as Senad el-Sadik el-Ureybi later claimed responsibility.
label: sentence

sentence: Gaddafi's son Mutassim, who had also been among the convoy, was also captured, and found dead several hours later, most probably from an extrajudicial execution.
label: sentence

sentence: Around 140 Gaddafi loyalists were rounded up from the convoy; tied up and abused, the corpses of 66 were found at the nearby Mahari Hotel, victims of extrajudicial execution.
label: sentence

sentence: Libya's chief forensic pathologist, Dr. Othman al-Zintani, carried out the autopsies of Gaddafi, his son and Jabr in the days following their deaths; although the pathologist initially told the press that Gaddafi had died from a gunshot wound to the head, the autopsy report was not made public.
label: sentence

sentence: On the afternoon of Gaddafi's death, NTC Prime Minister Mahmoud Jibril publicly revealed the news.
label: sentence

sentence: Gaddafi's corpse was placed in the freezer of a local market alongside the corpses of Yunis Jabr and Mutassim; the bodies were publicly displayed for four days, with Libyans from all over the country coming to view them.
label: sentence

sentence: In response to international calls, on 24 October Jibril announced that a commission would investigate Gaddafi's death.
label: sentence

sentence: The pits and lands themselves do not directly represent the zeros and ones of binary data.

sentence: Instead, non-return-to-zero, inverted encoding is used: a change from pit to land or land to pit indicates a one, while no change indicates a series of zeros.

sentence: This in turn is decoded by reversing the eight-to-fourteen modulation used in mastering the disc, and then reversing the cross-interleaved Reed–Solomon coding, finally revealing the raw data stored on the disc.

sentence: A transistor is a semiconductor device used to amplify or switch electronic signals and electrical power.
label: sentence

sentence: It is composed of semiconductor material with at least three terminals for connection to an external circuit.
label: sentence

sentence: A voltage or current applied to one pair of the transistor's terminals changes the current through another pair of terminals.
label: sentence

sentence: Because the controlled (output) power can be higher than the controlling (input) power, a transistor can amplify a signal.
label: sentence

sentence: Today, some transistors are packaged individually, but many more are found embedded in integrated circuits.
label: sentence

sentence: The transistor is the fundamental building block of modern electronic devices, and is ubiquitous in modern electronic systems.
label: sentence

sentence: First conceived by Julius Lilienfeld in 1926 and practically implemented in 1947 by American physicists John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley, the transistor revolutionized the field of electronics, and paved the way for smaller and cheaper radios, calculators, and computers, among other things.
label: sentence

sentence: The transistor is on the list of IEEE milestones in electronics, and Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for their achievement.
label: sentence

sentence: The thermionic triode, a vacuum tube invented in 1907, enabled amplified radio technology and long-distance telephony.
label: sentence

sentence: The triode, however, was a fragile device that consumed a lot of power.
label: sentence

sentence: Physicist Julius Edgar Lilienfeld filed a patent for a field-effect transistor (FET) in Canada in 1925, which was intended to be a solid-state replacement for the triode.
label: sentence

sentence: Lilienfeld also filed identical patents in the United States in 1926 and 1928.
label: sentence

sentence: However, Lilienfeld did not publish any research articles about his devices nor did his patents cite any specific examples of a working prototype.
label: sentence

sentence: Because the production of high-quality semiconductor materials was still decades away, Lilienfeld's solid-state amplifier ideas would not have found practical use in the 1920s and 1930s, even if such a device had been built.
label: sentence

sentence: In 1934, German inventor Oskar Heil patented a similar device.
label: sentence

sentence: From November 17, 1947 to December 23, 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain at AT&T's Bell Labs in the United States performed experiments and observed that when two gold point contacts were applied to a crystal of germanium, a signal was produced with the output power greater than the input.
label: sentence

sentence: Solid State Physics Group leader William Shockley saw the potential in this, and over the next few months worked to greatly expand the knowledge of semiconductors.
label: sentence

sentence: The term transistor was coined by John R. Pierce as a contraction of the term transresistance.
label: sentence

sentence: According to Lillian Hoddeson and Vicki Daitch, authors of a biography of John Bardeen, Shockley had proposed that Bell Labs' first patent for a transistor should be based on the field-effect and that he be named as the inventor.
label: sentence

sentence: Having unearthed Lilienfeld’s patents that went into obscurity years earlier, lawyers at Bell Labs advised against Shockley's proposal because the idea of a field-effect transistor that used an electric field as a "grid" was not new.
label: sentence

sentence: Instead, what Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley invented in 1947 was the first point-contact transistor.
label: sentence

sentence: In acknowledgement of this accomplishment, Shockley, Bardeen, and Brattain were jointly awarded the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics "for their researches on semiconductors and their discovery of the transistor effect."
label: sentence

sentence: In 1948, the point-contact transistor was independently invented by German physicists Herbert Mataré and Heinrich Welker while working at the Compagnie des Freins et Signaux, a Westinghouse subsidiary located in Paris.
label: sentence

sentence: Mataré had previous experience in developing crystal rectifiers from silicon and germanium in the German radar effort during World War II.
label: sentence

sentence: Using this knowledge, he began researching the phenomenon of "interference" in 1947.
label: sentence

sentence: By June 1948, witnessing currents flowing through point-contacts, Mataré produced consistent results using samples of germanium produced by Welker, similar to what Bardeen and Brattain had accomplished earlier in December 1947.
label: sentence

sentence: Realizing that Bell Labs' scientists had already invented the transistor before them, the company rushed to get its "transistron" into production for amplified use in France's telephone network.
label: sentence

sentence: Although several companies each produce over a billion individually packaged (known as discrete) transistors every year, the vast majority of transistors are now produced in integrated circuits (often shortened to IC, microchips or simply chips), along with diodes, resistors, capacitors and other electronic components, to produce complete electronic circuits.
label: sentence

sentence: A logic gate consists of up to about twenty transistors whereas an advanced microprocessor, as of 2009, can use as many as 3 billion transistors (MOSFETs).
label: sentence

sentence: "About 60 million transistors were built in 2002… for [each] man, woman, and child on Earth."

sentence: The essential usefulness of a transistor comes from its ability to use a small signal applied between one pair of its terminals to control a much larger signal at another pair of terminals.
label: sentence

sentence: This property is called gain.
label: sentence

sentence: It can produce a stronger output signal, a voltage or current, which is proportional to a weaker input signal; that is, it can act as an amplifier.
label: sentence

sentence: Alternatively, the transistor can be used to turn current on or off in a circuit as an electrically controlled switch, where the amount of current is determined by other circuit elements.
label: sentence

sentence: There are two types of transistors, which have slight differences in how they are used in a circuit.
label: sentence

sentence: A bipolar transistor has terminals labeled base, collector, and emitter.
label: sentence

sentence: A small current at the base terminal (that is, flowing between the base and the emitter) can control or switch a much larger current between the collector and emitter terminals.
label: sentence

sentence: For a field-effect transistor, the terminals are labeled gate, source, and drain, and a voltage at the gate can control a current between source and drain.
label: sentence

sentence: In a grounded-emitter transistor circuit, such as the light-switch circuit shown, as the base voltage rises, the emitter and collector currents rise exponentially.
label: sentence

sentence: The collector voltage drops because of reduced resistance from collector to emitter.
label: sentence

sentence: If the voltage difference between the collector and emitter were zero (or near zero), the collector current would be limited only by the load resistance (light bulb) and the supply voltage.
label: sentence

sentence: This is called saturation because current is flowing from collector to emitter freely.
label: sentence

sentence: When saturated, the switch is said to be on.
label: sentence

sentence: Providing sufficient base drive current is a key problem in the use of bipolar transistors as switches.
label: sentence

sentence: The transistor provides current gain, allowing a relatively large current in the collector to be switched by a much smaller current into the base terminal.
label: sentence

sentence: The ratio of these currents varies depending on the type of transistor, and even for a particular type, varies depending on the collector current.
label: sentence

sentence: In the example light-switch circuit shown, the resistor is chosen to provide enough base current to ensure the transistor will be saturated.
label: sentence

sentence: In a switching circuit, the idea is to simulate, as near as possible, the ideal switch having the properties of open circuit when off, short circuit when on, and an instantaneous transition between the two states.
label: sentence

sentence: Parameters are chosen such that the "off" output is limited to leakage currents too small to affect connected circuitry; the resistance of the transistor in the "on" state is too small to affect circuitry; and the transition between the two states is fast enough not to have a detrimental effect.
label: sentence

sentence: Bipolar transistors are so named because they conduct by using both majority and minority carriers.
label: sentence

sentence: The bipolar junction transistor, the first type of transistor to be mass-produced, is a combination of two junction diodes, and is formed of either a thin layer of p-type semiconductor sandwiched between two n-type semiconductors (an n–p–n transistor), or a thin layer of n-type semiconductor sandwiched between two p-type semiconductors (a p–n–p transistor).
label: sentence

sentence: This construction produces two p–n junctions: a base–emitter junction and a base–collector junction, separated by a thin region of semiconductor known as the base region (two junction diodes wired together without sharing an intervening semiconducting region will not make a transistor).
label: sentence

sentence: BJTs have three terminals, corresponding to the three layers of semiconductor—an emitter, a base, and a collector.
label: sentence

sentence: They are useful in amplifiers because the currents at the emitter and collector are controllable by a relatively small base current.
label: sentence

sentence: In an n–p–n transistor operating in the active region, the emitter–base junction is forward biased (electrons and holes recombine at the junction), and electrons are injected into the base region.
label: sentence

sentence: Because the base is narrow, most of these electrons will diffuse into the reverse-biased (electrons and holes are formed at, and move away from the junction) base–collector junction and be swept into the collector; perhaps one-hundredth of the electrons will recombine in the base, which is the dominant mechanism in the base current.
label: sentence

sentence: By controlling the number of electrons that can leave the base, the number of electrons entering the collector can be controlled.
label: sentence

sentence: Collector current is approximately β (common-emitter current gain) times the base current.
label: sentence

sentence: It is typically greater than 100 for small-signal transistors but can be smaller in transistors designed for high-power applications.
label: sentence

sentence: In a FET, the drain-to-source current flows via a conducting channel that connects the source region to the drain region.
label: sentence

sentence: The conductivity is varied by the electric field that is produced when a voltage is applied between the gate and source terminals; hence the current flowing between the drain and source is controlled by the voltage applied between the gate and source.
label: sentence

sentence: As the gate–source voltage (VGS) is increased, the drain–source current (IDS) increases exponentially for VGS below threshold, and then at a roughly quadratic rate (IGS ∝ (VGS − VT)2) (where VT is the threshold voltage at which drain current begins) in the "space-charge-limited" region above threshold.
label: sentence

sentence: A quadratic behavior is not observed in modern devices, for example, at the 65 nm technology node.
label: sentence

sentence: FETs are divided into two families: junction FET (JFET) and insulated gate FET (IGFET).
label: sentence

sentence: The IGFET is more commonly known as a metal–oxide–semiconductor FET (MOSFET), reflecting its original construction from layers of metal (the gate), oxide (the insulation), and semiconductor.
label: sentence

sentence: Unlike IGFETs, the JFET gate forms a p–n diode with the channel which lies between the source and drain.
label: sentence

sentence: Functionally, this makes the n-channel JFET the solid-state equivalent of the vacuum tube triode which, similarly, forms a diode between its grid and cathode.
label: sentence

sentence: Also, both devices operate in the depletion mode, they both have a high input impedance, and they both conduct current under the control of an input voltage.
label: sentence

sentence: FETs are further divided into depletion-mode and enhancement-mode types, depending on whether the channel is turned on or off with zero gate-to-source voltage.
label: sentence

sentence: For enhancement mode, the channel is off at zero bias, and a gate potential can "enhance" the conduction.
label: sentence

sentence: For the depletion mode, the channel is on at zero bias, and a gate potential (of the opposite polarity) can "deplete" the channel, reducing conduction.
label: sentence

sentence: For either mode, a more positive gate voltage corresponds to a higher current for n-channel devices and a lower current for p-channel devices.
label: sentence

sentence: Nearly all JFETs are depletion-mode because the diode junctions would forward bias and conduct if they were enhancement-mode devices; most IGFETs are enhancement-mode types.
label: sentence

sentence: The bipolar junction transistor (BJT) was the most commonly used transistor in the 1960s and 70s.
label: sentence

sentence: Even after MOSFETs became widely available, the BJT remained the transistor of choice for many analog circuits such as amplifiers because of their greater linearity and ease of manufacture.
label: sentence

sentence: In integrated circuits, the desirable properties of MOSFETs allowed them to capture nearly all market share for digital circuits.
label: sentence

sentence: Discrete MOSFETs can be applied in transistor applications, including analog circuits, voltage regulators, amplifiers, power transmitters and motor drivers.

sentence: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves which carry signals through the air (or through space) at the speed of light with almost no transmission loss.
label: sentence

sentence: Radio transmitters and receivers are used to convey signals (information) in systems including broadcast (audio) radio, television, mobile telephones, Wi-Fi (WLAN) data networks, trunk lines and point-to-point communications links (telephone, data networks), satellite links, many remote controlled devices such as garage door openers, and wireless remote sensors, among many others.
label: sentence

sentence: Radio waves are also used directly for measurements in technologies including radar, GPS, and radio astronomy.
label: sentence

sentence: In each and every case, the transmitters and receivers involved require antennas, although these are sometimes hidden (such as the antenna inside an AM radio or inside a laptop computer equipped with Wi-Fi).
label: sentence

sentence: One example of omnidirectional antennas is the very common vertical antenna or whip antenna consisting of a metal rod (often, but not always, a quarter of a wavelength long).

sentence: A dipole antenna is similar but consists of two such conductors extending in opposite directions, with a total length that is often, but not always, a half of a wavelength long.

sentence: Dipoles are typically oriented horizontally in which case they are weakly directional: signals are reasonably well radiated toward or received from all directions with the exception of the direction along the conductor itself; this region is called the antenna blind cone or null.

sentence: Both the vertical and dipole antennas are simple in construction and relatively inexpensive.

sentence: The dipole antenna, which is the basis for most antenna designs, is a balanced component, with equal but opposite voltages and currents applied at its two terminals through a balanced transmission line (or to a coaxial transmission line through a so-called balun).

sentence: The vertical antenna, on the other hand, is a monopole antenna.

sentence: It is typically connected to the inner conductor of a coaxial transmission line (or a matching network); the shield of the transmission line is connected to ground.

sentence: Antennas more complex than the dipole or vertical designs are usually intended to increase the directivity and consequently the gain of the antenna.

sentence: This can be accomplished in many different ways leading to a plethora of antenna designs.

sentence: A necessary condition for the aforementioned reciprocity property is that the materials in the antenna and transmission medium are linear and reciprocal.

sentence: Reciprocal (or bilateral) means that the material has the same response to an electric current or magnetic field in one direction, as it has to the field or current in the opposite direction.

sentence: Antennas are characterized by a number of performance measures which a user would be concerned with in selecting or designing an antenna for a particular application.
label: sentence

sentence: Chief among these relate to the directional characteristics (as depicted in the antenna's radiation pattern) and the resulting gain.
label: sentence

sentence: The antenna's power gain (or simply "gain") also takes into account the antenna's efficiency, and is often the primary figure of merit.

sentence: Resonant antennas are expected to be used around a particular resonant frequency; an antenna must therefore be built or ordered to match the frequency range of the intended application.

sentence: The physical size of an antenna is often a practical issue, particularly at lower frequencies (longer wavelengths).

sentence: Highly directional antennas need to be significantly larger than the wavelength.

label: sentence

sentence: Fortunately at higher frequencies (UHF, microwaves) trading off performance to obtain a smaller physical size is usually not required.

sentence: The majority of antenna designs are based on the resonance principle.
label: sentence

sentence: This relies on the behaviour of moving electrons, which reflect off surfaces where the dielectric constant changes, in a fashion similar to the way light reflects when optical properties change.
label: sentence

sentence: In these designs, the reflective surface is created by the end of a conductor, normally a thin metal wire or rod, which in the simplest case has a feed point at one end where it is connected to a transmission line.
label: sentence

sentence: The conductor, or element, is aligned with the electrical field of the desired signal, normally meaning it is perpendicular to the line from the antenna to the source (or receiver in the case of a broadcast antenna).
label: sentence

sentence: The radio signal's electrical component induces a voltage in the conductor.
label: sentence

sentence: This causes an electrical current to begin flowing in the direction of the signal's instantaneous field.
label: sentence

sentence: When the resulting current reaches the end of the conductor, it reflects, which is equivalent to a 180 degree change in phase.
label: sentence

sentence: If the conductor is 1⁄4 of a wavelength long, current from the feed point will undergo 90 degree phase change by the time it reaches the end of the conductor, reflect through 180 degrees, and then another 90 degrees as it travels back.
label: sentence

sentence: That means it has undergone a total 360 degree phase change, returning it to the original signal.
label: sentence

sentence: The current in the element thus adds to the current being created from the source at that instant.
label: sentence

sentence: This process creates a standing wave in the conductor, with the maximum current at the feed.
label: sentence

sentence: The ordinary half-wave dipole is probably the most widely used antenna design.
label: sentence

sentence: This consists of two 1⁄4-wavelength elements arranged end-to-end, and lying along essentially the same axis (or collinear), each feeding one side of a two-conductor transmission wire.
label: sentence

sentence: The physical arrangement of the two elements places them 180 degrees out of phase, which means that at any given instant one of the elements is driving current into the transmission line while the other is pulling it out.
label: sentence

sentence: The monopole antenna is essentially one half of the half-wave dipole, a single 1⁄4-wavelength element with the other side connected to ground or an equivalent ground plane (or counterpoise).
label: sentence

sentence: Monopoles, which are one-half the size of a dipole, are common for long-wavelength radio signals where a dipole would be impractically large.
label: sentence

sentence: Another common design is the folded dipole, which is essentially two dipoles placed side-by-side and connected at their ends to make a single one-wavelength antenna.

sentence: The standing wave forms with this desired pattern at the design frequency, f0, and antennas are normally designed to be this size.

sentence: However, feeding that element with 3f0 (whose wavelength is 1⁄3 that of f0) will also lead to a standing wave pattern.

sentence: Thus, an antenna element is also resonant when its length is 3⁄4 of a wavelength.

sentence: This is true for all odd multiples of 1⁄4 wavelength.

sentence: This allows some flexibility of design in terms of antenna lengths and feed points.

sentence: Antennas used in such a fashion are known to be harmonically operated.

sentence: The quarter-wave elements imitate a series-resonant electrical element due to the standing wave present along the conductor.
label: sentence

sentence: At the resonant frequency, the standing wave has a current peak and voltage node (minimum) at the feed.

sentence: In electrical terms, this means the element has minimum reactance, generating the maximum current for minimum voltage.

sentence: This is the ideal situation, because it produces the maximum output for the minimum input, producing the highest possible efficiency.

sentence: Contrary to an ideal (lossless) series-resonant circuit, a finite resistance remains (corresponding to the relatively small voltage at the feed-point) due to the antenna's radiation resistance as well as any actual electrical losses.

sentence: It is possible to use the impedance matching concepts to construct vertical antennas substantially shorter than the 1⁄4 wavelength at which the antenna is resonant.

sentence: Gain is a parameter which measures the degree of directivity of the antenna's radiation pattern.
label: sentence

sentence: A high-gain antenna will radiate most of its power in a particular direction, while a low-gain antenna will radiate over a wider angle.
label: sentence

sentence: The antenna gain, or power gain of an antenna is defined as the ratio of the intensity (power per unit surface area)  radiated by the antenna in the direction of its maximum output, at an arbitrary distance, divided by the intensity  radiated at the same distance by a hypothetical isotropic antenna which radiates equal power in all directions.
label: sentence

sentence: This dimensionless ratio is usually expressed logarithmically in decibels, these units are called "decibels-isotropic" (dBi)
label: sentence

sentence: High-gain antennas have the advantage of longer range and better signal quality, but must be aimed carefully at the other antenna.
label: sentence

sentence: An example of a high-gain antenna is a parabolic dish such as a satellite television antenna.
label: sentence

sentence: Low-gain antennas have shorter range, but the orientation of the antenna is relatively unimportant.
label: sentence

sentence: An example of a low-gain antenna is the whip antenna found on portable radios and cordless phones.

sentence: Antenna gain should not be confused with amplifier gain, a separate parameter measuring the increase in signal power due to an amplifying device.

sentence: The radiation pattern of an antenna is a plot of the relative field strength of the radio waves emitted by the antenna at different angles.
label: sentence

sentence: It is typically represented by a three-dimensional graph, or polar plots of the horizontal and vertical cross sections.
label: sentence

sentence: The pattern of an ideal isotropic antenna, which radiates equally in all directions, would look like a sphere.
label: sentence

sentence: Many nondirectional antennas, such as monopoles and dipoles, emit equal power in all horizontal directions, with the power dropping off at higher and lower angles; this is called an omnidirectional pattern and when plotted looks like a torus or donut.
label: sentence

sentence: The radiation of many antennas shows a pattern of maxima or "lobes" at various angles, separated by "nulls", angles where the radiation falls to zero.
label: sentence

sentence: This is because the radio waves emitted by different parts of the antenna typically interfere, causing maxima at angles where the radio waves arrive at distant points in phase, and zero radiation at other angles where the radio waves arrive out of phase.
label: sentence

sentence: In a directional antenna designed to project radio waves in a particular direction, the lobe in that direction is designed larger than the others and is called the "main lobe".
label: sentence

sentence: The other lobes usually represent unwanted radiation and are called "sidelobes".
label: sentence

sentence: The axis through the main lobe is called the "principal axis" or "boresight axis".

sentence: As an electro-magnetic wave travels through the different parts of the antenna system (radio, feed line, antenna, free space) it may encounter differences in impedance (E/H, V/I, etc.).
label: sentence

sentence: At each interface, depending on the impedance match, some fraction of the wave's energy will reflect back to the source, forming a standing wave in the feed line.
label: sentence

sentence: The ratio of maximum power to minimum power in the wave can be measured and is called the standing wave ratio (SWR).
label: sentence

sentence: A SWR of 1:1 is ideal.
label: sentence

sentence: A SWR of 1.5:1 is considered to be marginally acceptable in low power applications where power loss is more critical, although an SWR as high as 6:1 may still be usable with the right equipment.
label: sentence

sentence: Minimizing impedance differences at each interface (impedance matching) will reduce SWR and maximize power transfer through each part of the antenna system.

sentence: Efficiency of a transmitting antenna is the ratio of power actually radiated (in all directions) to the power absorbed by the antenna terminals.
label: sentence

sentence: The power supplied to the antenna terminals which is not radiated is converted into heat.
label: sentence

sentence: This is usually through loss resistance in the antenna's conductors, but can also be due to dielectric or magnetic core losses in antennas (or antenna systems) using such components.
label: sentence

sentence: Such loss effectively robs power from the transmitter, requiring a stronger transmitter in order to transmit a signal of a given strength.
label: sentence

sentence: For instance, if a transmitter delivers 100 W into an antenna having an efficiency of 80%, then the antenna will radiate 80 W as radio waves and produce 20 W of heat.
label: sentence

sentence: In order to radiate 100 W of power, one would need to use a transmitter capable of supplying 125 W to the antenna.
label: sentence

sentence: Note that antenna efficiency is a separate issue from impedance matching, which may also reduce the amount of power radiated using a given transmitter.
label: sentence

sentence: If an SWR meter reads 150 W of incident power and 50 W of reflected power, that means that 100 W have actually been absorbed by the antenna (ignoring transmission line losses).
label: sentence

sentence: How much of that power has actually been radiated cannot be directly determined through electrical measurements at (or before) the antenna terminals, but would require (for instance) careful measurement of field strength.
label: sentence

sentence: Fortunately the loss resistance of antenna conductors such as aluminum rods can be calculated and the efficiency of an antenna using such materials predicted.
label: sentence

sentence: However loss resistance will generally affect the feedpoint impedance, adding to its resistive (real) component.
label: sentence

sentence: That resistance will consist of the sum of the radiation resistance Rr and the loss resistance Rloss.
label: sentence

sentence: If an rms current I is delivered to the terminals of an antenna, then a power of I2Rr will be radiated and a power of I2Rloss will be lost as heat.
label: sentence

sentence: Therefore, the efficiency of an antenna is equal to Rr / (Rr + Rloss).
label: sentence

sentence: Of course only the total resistance Rr + Rloss can be directly measured.
label: sentence

sentence: According to reciprocity, the efficiency of an antenna used as a receiving antenna is identical to the efficiency as defined above.

sentence: The power that an antenna will deliver to a receiver (with a proper impedance match) is reduced by the same amount.

sentence: In some receiving applications, the very inefficient antennas may have little impact on performance.

sentence: The flowering plants (angiosperms), also known as Angiospermae or Magnoliophyta, are the most diverse group of land plants, with about 350,000 species.

sentence: Etymologically, angiosperm means a plant that produces seeds within an enclosure, in other words, a fruiting plant.

sentence: Fossilized spores suggest that higher plants (embryophytes) have lived on land for at least 475 million years.

sentence: The apparently sudden appearance of nearly modern flowers in the fossil record initially posed such a problem for the theory of evolution that it was called an "abominable mystery" by Charles Darwin.
